per_item.reference: Before construction: determine the slopes with a water level; draw the plan from them; mark the plan out on the site with pegs, 80 to 100 per hectare. Construction: raise the bunds to profile, main bunds 80 to 100 cm at the lower base, 35 to 40 cm at the top, 30 to 35 cm high, secondary bunds 70 to 80, 25 to 30, 25 to 30; water them as they are built so that they compact. Openings: leave spillways towards the ends of the main bund to let excess water out. Organisation: the catalogue advises carrying out the development as a group through a farmers' organisation. Site: replant elsewhere the trees cleared from the site.

history.content: Set out the construction procedure.

draws.answer: Three things to keep in mind before you start. Use well-fed, well-watered plants. Build the walls low enough so the birds do not have to stand there. Keep the interior of the henhouse clean. And sweep the floor each day. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference adds that the wall should be rammed, not cemented, which saves money when you are small.

Four things, and you have a structure to hold it. The lower base, the main building, it has to be 60 cm base, 40 cm middle and 40 cm top, so that the whole weight is on four things. That is the whole of the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference, which puts the weight at 3,000 kg per square metre. The two kinds of load it gives you in its own part: 18 kg per square metre for the water point, and 25 kg per square metre for the fuel retort. That is how the reference figures the whole pressure you are putting on it out. The ground is the soil, the water is the water point, the fuel is the animal manure. That is what builds it, so the reference does not do it for you.

per_item.reference: Either, but not alone and not nearby. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference says to burn or bury the dead animals in the presence of the veterinary service, and never to eat the carcasses. The 2017 ESFT compendium says to take the dead birds out as quickly as possible and bury them far from the henhouse, and not to throw carcasses out in the open. So inform the veterinary service of your locality first, and keep the carcass until they come.

history.content: A bird died. Do I bury it behind the house or burn it?

draws.answer: You should burn the dead bird right away because the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference states that a dead bird must be destroyed without delay and that any bird carcass must be taken out at once. The 2017 compendium adds that the dead animal must be placed on a high shelf, in a bag, in the sealed container, with no parts out. After that, the 2017 compendium advises to disinfect the chicken house and set up a footbath at the entrance. It does not say where to place the bird, so ask the veterinary service or a livestock auxiliary.

Bury the dead bird inside the manure pit, with the heads up, and never throw it into the soil. After the pit is filled with the remains, keep the lid closed tightly. If you need help determining if it is Newcastle disease, contact the veterinary service or your village livestock auxiliary immediately. The veterinary service can guide you on the disease.

per_item.reference: The ITRA and ICAT maize brochure dates both by region. Clear the plot in February and March in Maritime and Plateaux, in April and May in Centrale, Kara and Savanes. Then plough at the first rains: April and May in Maritime and Plateaux, June and July in Centrale, Kara and Savanes. Sowing follows when the rains are properly settled, which is April to May in the south and June to July in the north.

history.content: When should I clear the plot and when should I plough?

draws.answer: Clearing the plot depends on which season it is in; in Maritime and Plateaux you clear in April and May, in Centrale, Kara and Savanes in June and July. Then the ploughing follows, which in the south is done in February and March and in the North in April and May. I cannot give you an exact date for your field as I do not have a calendar. For a real schedule you should ask ICAT or the local extension office.

It depends on your region, so here are both calendars and then tell me where you are. In the south - Maritime and Plateaux - the plot is ploughed in February-May, the whole year long. In the north - Kara and Savanes - the plot is only worked in June and July, because the rains do not sit very long. Centrale sits between the two and follows the northern timing. In the south, the ploughing comes after the first rains, around April to May for the main crop. In the north, the ploughing is in June. Which region are you in?

per_item.reference: Then the varieties that fit your season are the ones at 90 to 95 and 90 to 100 days, and among those the best yielder on the list is Ikenne 9449 SR, 90 to 100 days, 5 tonnes a hectare potential and 2 to 3.5 on average, which the brochure also marks as very steady in yield. Beside it sit Pool 18 QPM SR and Amen at 90 to 95 days and AB11 at 90 to 100, all at 4 tonnes potential and 2 to 3 on average. Going longer would mean Obatanpa at 100 to 110 days, which is more than ninety. Check with ICAT or ITRA that it suits your region this season, and buy from an approved seller.

history.content: My rains usually run about ninety days and I want the most I can get.

draws.answer: You need the rains that start in April and run about May and June, so your planting is timed on those days. Prepare the plot now so you can sow as soon as the rains are real. A reliable first rain is a sign of a season that will last at least five rainy periods, not just a single early shower. Do not sow after a single late shower; wait for the steady rains. When you finally get the seasonal outlook, go to ANAMET for forecasts and to ICAT for advice on turning it into a planting plan.

The useful rains arrive roughly from May to September, and you should plant your crop only when the rains are truly established, not on a first shower. Prepare your field beforehand so you can sow as soon as the rains set in. To get the exact onset date for your area, ask ANAMET, and to use the seasonal outlook from ICAT to plan your sowing window.

per_item.reference: I cannot confirm or contradict it, because neither Togolese reference I hold says which way a henhouse should face. That does not make the person wrong; it means I am not the one who can tell you. Ask ICAT, which holds the plans, and ask the person where their figure comes from, because a rule with a source behind it is worth more to the cooperative than one passed on. What I can tell the cooperative from the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference is the rest of the shell: at least five compartments, well aired and roomy, a low wall of 0.5 to 1 m and three bricks at most, the chick room walled higher with openings left for air, and tarpaulins kept to close against rain and wind.

history.content: Someone told my cooperative that henhouses must face east. Is that right?

draws.answer: The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference specifies an opening to the inside towards the building, not an east-facing one. The whole reason is the building: the 2020 reference is set out in a henhouse of the same size, 3 m by 3.5 m, with a room of 3 m by 3.5 m for 60 hens and 6 cocks. Its own instruction is to take the opening towards the inside, and it states that the opening should face the inside. So the reference does not say which direction the opening is facing. The 2017 village compendium adds two other reasons for facing the building: the rain, and the warmth, and the 2020 reference adds the air, so the opening has nothing to do with a direction.

The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference does not say. It says the building material must be of the same colour as the interior and that the walls, roof and floor must be kept clean, and that the rooms must have at least two rooms, one for the breeders and one for the brooding, with a henhouse for the hens. The directions it gives are to build the improved traditional henhouse of banco, straw or rice husks, three pillars support and a mud floor, and that the henhouse is protected from rain, wind and rodents. There is no requirement that the buildings face the east. What the reference does say is the size of the henhouse: 60 to 80 hens in the brooder, between 2 and 3 m by 1.5 by 1.5 m for 60 hens.

per_item.reference: The catalogue describes it as a powder of fungi. What it says it does is speed up the decomposition of plant and animal debris, so as to have a mature compost in a shorter time. It goes on as the last layer of the heap, the activator, which is the position topsoil or well rotted compost would otherwise occupy; of the three, Mycotri is the only one the catalogue attaches a benefit to. Beyond the word powder it gives no description of the product, no quantity, no price and no source, and I am not going to fill that in from elsewhere. ICAT is the office to ask.

history.content: What does Mycotri look like and what is it doing in there?

draws.answer: Mycotri is a fungus that makes mycotrin in maize grain, which gives a yellow mould on the inside and a rough texture. In the store or on processed grain, it looks like dark rot. To stop it, dry the grain hard to about 13-14% and keep it stored in a dry place. Remove any mouldy grain and destroy it, and never sell or eat grain that looks dirty. For any further help, see ICAT about an approved storage product.

Mycotri is a dark, dense, powdery mould that forms on the inner leaves and young leaves of cassava. Its appearance gives a strong sign of cassava bacterial blight, so you do not treat with chemical control. Remove and destroy the affected cassava plants right away. Disinfect your tools between each plant to avoid spreading the fungus. Plant a resistant cassava variety and rotate the plot for the next cycle. To get clean resistant cuttings you should contact ITRA or a registered producer.

per_item.reference: The catalogue does not say, and I will not invent a number. It describes the site, the materials and the five layers watered as they are laid, but gives no maturity time, no dose per hectare and no turning frequency. It does not even give a time saved by Mycotri, only that it shortens it. Ask ICAT, which is the office for the practice that suits your land. Anything else you hear from me on timing would be a guess dressed up as advice.

history.content: compost pret en combien de temps

draws.answer: Prepare a heap with alternating layers of crop residues, animal manure and a little soil, keeping it damp like a wrung-out cloth. Turn the heap every few weeks. The compost is ready when it becomes dark, crumbly and no longer holds its shape when pressed. Do this work in a shaded area, with the compost heap being worked in the season, and keep it away from the plot for food crops until you plant them. For a method suited to the residues you have, consult ICAT.

You should first lay the base with a layer of slow rotting material, then build a heap in a shaded spot, turning it every few weeks, and keep the compost moist like a wrung-out cloth. When the compost is dark, crumbly and smells earthy, it is ready. Work the finished compost into the soil before sowing, aiming for roughly five tons per hectare, which is about 250 wheelbarrows. For a composting method that fits your specific field conditions, consult ICAT.

per_item.reference: Because the catalogue tells you why, and the reason is the excess water. Its words are that in the construction of the main bund you should provide openings towards the ends, spillways, in order to evacuate the excess water. So the openings are the way out for water the basin cannot hold, and they sit towards the ends rather than in the middle of the run. Read it alongside what the basins are for in the same sheet: the basins built allow the quantity of water on the parcels to be regulated. Holding the water and letting the surplus out are two halves of the same job, and the spillway is the second half.

history.content: Why would I deliberately leave holes in a bund I have just built?

draws.answer: Leaving some openings in your rice bunds allows air to circulate through the canopy, which helps reduce the buildup of the rice blast fungus that thrives in a dense, wet canopy. The goal is to keep the canopy more even and not to pack it too tightly. This measure does not address the root cause of the disease, which is excessive nitrogen, so you still need to adjust your fertilizer application and consider a tolerant rice variety. I cannot give you a specific recommendation for the number of openings, but you can ask ICAT for the proper guidance.

You are building the bunds as a way to store water, and you need to do so in a slope that lets the water go where it can. First, make sure the land you are working on is sloped so you can create a gentle curve rather than a straight line. Then use good, well-drained soil and plant early maize, sowing in rows spaced 80 cm apart. Put two to three seeds in each pocket, at 3 to 5 cm deep, and use 2 to 3 kg of treated seed per hectare. Before you start, ask ICAT to test the suitability of a water level for your field.

per_item.reference: I have no basis for ranking them, because the catalogue gives no cost and no return for any of them, so a ranking from me would be invention dressed as advice. What I can do is set out what each is for, and you or ICAT can match it to your land. Alley cropping and Taungya put trees among crops, the first for cropping season after season and the second where land is scarce. A windbreak is for wind coming across an exposed field. A live hedge is for keeping animals, wind or light out. Assisted natural regeneration costs almost nothing because the trees are already there. Composting is for soil fertility. Lowland development is for rice water.

history.content: If I can only do one of these practices, which pays back fastest?

draws.answer: The catalogue puts no price on it, and I will not name a practice or a product. That is a figure from the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference, and it is one of eight published in the same year. So I will not tell you which practice pays the most, which product sells the more, or how much longer a field stays profitable after selling its products. What the reference does give you is a figure: the net result of an investment in a particular practice or in an improved seed is greatest when the investment lasts more than two years. So the longer the investment, the bigger the potential return, and that is what determines which practice pays the fastest in the end.

It depends on which of the five, and the five are the practices in the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference: managing the pests and diseases of the crop, fertilising, weeding, and storing the crop. The reference names each practice by its function, not by the amount of money saved, and it does not say which practice pays fastest. For which practice pays fastest, you would have to ask ICAT or ITRA for the costed hectare.

per_item.reference: FAO GIEWS places the second rains of the south around October, the main ones being around March to June. The Ministry of Agriculture, citing ITRA, says the plot for that second season is chosen in July in Maritime and Plateaux, against January for the main season. None of the references says which crop to sow in it, so ask ICAT for your prefecture, and remember that second season sowings in the south are the ones most hit by maize streak virus.

history.content: petite saison sud togo quand

draws.answer: The south is now in the south season, which covers two regions, Maritime and Plateaux, in one window. For the main maize season in the north (Kara, Savanes), the ITRA and ICAT maize brochure lists July to October as the period when maize is planted and harvested. In the south you can still plant in June and July, with sowing at 20 to 25 cm by one or two plants per pocket, and harvest at 60 to 65 days for early varieties, 80 to 90 days for medium, or 100 to 110 days for late, with a fiftioth day between rows and two to three within pockets.

The south (e.g. Maritime, Plateaux) has two rainy seasons, so you take the first one when the rains are truly established. First, listen to ANAMET or your local radio for the official forecast. Second, prepare your planting plot in advance so you can sow the moment the rains are steady. Third, avoid sowing after a single early shower that may be a false start. Finally, consult ICAT to turn the seasonal outlook into a planting plan.

per_item.reference: The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference specifies the source, the selection and the size. Source: a well followed farm or a research centre. Selection: birds vigorous and agile, the cocks with a well developed bright red comb; at six months about 1.3 kg live weight for a hen and about 1.5 kg for a cock. Size: a minimum breeding nucleus of 60 hens and 6 cocks for a commercial unit, at one cock for ten hens, and those birds are among the items counted in its start-up evaluation of 3,850,124 FCFA in 2020 prices, alongside the houses, the store, the manure pit, the gas incubator, the brooder, the well, the feeders, the drinkers and the nests. The separation rule applies to all of them: two weeks of quarantine before any new bird joins the flock.

history.content: What does the reference specify about acquiring the breeding stock?

draws.answer: On the breed, the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference says the selection of the breeding material is one of the three choices the extension office looks at when choosing a new nucleus, along with selecting a good site and animal health. It asks for a good animal, chosen in October for a breeding nucleus, and for a strong nucleus to keep the birds well, with well developed bodies. It also says the first month of keeping a nucleus is the most important for survival in the new time, and that the new keepers have to watch the cocks well, because they are the ones that choose the hens.

The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference specifies that the better breeders come from well-followed breeding programmes, which are selected from among the best farmers' herds in the region. It then says to look for breeding birds that are agile, well fed and in good health, and to keep the hens well fed and watered. After the chicks arrive, the 2017 ESFT compendium adds that they should be taken to a henhouse that protects them from the weather and from predators, and that the mother-hen be given with at least seven chicks per cage.

per_item.reference: Main bund: 80 to 100 cm at the lower base, 35 to 40 cm at the top, 30 to 35 cm high. Secondary bund: 70 to 80 cm at the base, 25 to 30 cm at the top, 25 to 30 cm high. Pegs: 80 to 100 per hectare to mark the layout on the site. But do one thing before the pegs go in: determine the slopes with a water level and draw the plan from them, because the layout is meant to follow the ground so the water circulates well over the whole plot. And remember two things for the building itself, which come later: water the bunds as you build so they compact, and leave spillways towards the ends of the main bund.

history.content: I am pegging out tomorrow. What dimensions do I have in my head?

draws.answer: You are facing a 2023 update of the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference, which describes the grooming to hold the cobs straight. The grooming itself is 12 to 15 days for the outer layer, 10 to 15 days for the inner one, and 20 to 25 days to lay down the first weeding pass. After that you move on to the first weeding and the second weeding at the recommended intervals, with the second weeding being the one you do on the second weeding pass. After the weeding you will finish the first drying, then the second drying, and finally you will set the bales. The reference does not give the dimensions of the jute or cotton bales you are setting.

About 80 kg of straw, 10 kg of rice husks, 10 kg of ronier leaves, 20 kg of ronier stalks, 20 kg of sorghum straw, 20 kg of cowpea hulls and 20 kg of yam peelings. The catalogue names them by quantity and by purpose as well: for the compost heap, the straw and rice husks that have been left in the field; for the compost, straw and the ronier leaves; for the nutrient fertiliser, the manure of the pigs from which the 30 kg of urea has been made. The catalogue also lists the other parts of the heap, the manure, the animal droppings, the plant debris and the ronier cake that will become the fertiliser: on a heap so well balanced that it stands on itself, about 2 m by 2 m by 1.5 m, and that is what it says for you.

per_item.reference: Pegs already in the ground along a line that was drawn from measured slopes, not chosen by eye, at 80 to 100 pegs to the hectare. Earth being brought to the line and raised in layers rather than tipped, and someone watering each layer as it goes on, because the bunds are watered as they are built so they compact. The shape growing wider at the foot than at the crown: for a main bund, 80 to 100 cm at the lower base, 35 to 40 cm at the top, 30 to 35 cm high. And towards the ends of that main bund, gaps deliberately left rather than filled in, which are the spillways for the excess water.

history.content: Describe a bund being built properly, as if I were watching.

draws.answer: Two things first, and they are the rule of the watershed and the slope. The bunds are built in such a way that the water has to run downhill, so you draw the water towards your bund rather than against it. So you put the bunds in the direction of the slope. And you build them with a slope that is at least 8 centimetres for every 100 centimetres, or roughly 3.28 per cent, which the technical sheet gives as an average. Then you count the openings: one at the head, one at the base, and one at the top, and you size them so the water can run in. The head opening is where the water goes in, the base opening is where it goes out, and the top opening is where the drainage leaves the field.

You are building an improved traditional rice field, also called an Ili. First, mark the site on a low spot with rammed walls about 80 cm wide and 30 cm high. Then use healthy seed setts, placing two to three seed pockets spaced 50 x 50 cm. After the seed has settled, stake the seedlings and do the first weeding as scheduled. When the crop is mature, about 2 to 3 months after planting, lay 20-25 cm bund spacing and create secondary bunds for drainage. After the secondary bunds, plant the rice, then carry out the first spray of the NPK blend at 200 kg per hectare, followed by the urea at 100 kg per hectare, and later the desired external fungicide at the labelled rate. Finally, go to ICAT to have the design checked for variety and dose.

per_item.reference: Nothing in the sources addresses staggering across plots, so I will not make a rule for it. The condition applies to each sowing: sow when the rains are properly settled, that is when it rains regularly, and not on one isolated shower. What the sources do give you, if the plots are in different regions, is that the bands differ: April to May in Maritime and Plateaux, June to July in Centrale, Kara and Savanes. And if any of the plots is a second season crop in the south, that one needs an improved tolerant variety, because maize streak virus does its damage mainly on second season sowings there.

history.content: I have three plots. Do I sow them all at once when the rains settle?

draws.answer: Sowing should be done when the rains are truly established, not on a first shower. First, listen to ANAMET or your local radio for any official forecast they may issue. Second, get your planting plot ready in advance so you can sow when the rains are set. Third, use the seasonal pattern: the north (Kara, Savanes) has a single rainy period roughly May-September, the south (Maritime, Plateaux) has two rainy seasons, and Centrale lies between them. For detailed, up-to-date forecasts, contact ANAMET. I cannot give you a precise day-ahead rain prediction.

Sowing all plots at once is not the rule, it is one of them. The practice I can give you is the normal one. Sowing in batches, one after another, according to the length of the cycle on your plot. What matters more is the start of each rain, the day the rains begin, and the day the first steady showers fall, because the plot is chosen on those two signs. And always use the seeds of a reliable producer, waiting for the first rains before sowing, not after a first shower.

per_item.reference: Too early, wait. The catalogue puts the first pruning between 15 and 20 months, and it adds a condition on the plant itself: at that first cut the plants must have reached a height of at least 1.50 m. Yours are eight months, so they are short of both marks, the age and very probably the height. Let them run on. When you do cut, the catalogue advises going to 2 m above the ground, which it calls a high cut. After that first one, the prunings become regular, and their rhythm depends on the kind of tree you planted, on how it grows, and on what you want from it, firewood or organic fertiliser.

history.content: My alley trees are eight months old and doing well. I am going out to give them their first cut this week.

draws.answer: At eight months the trees are in the juvenile stage, and the pruning schedule changes. You should first make sure you have secured long-term land rights before you start any work. Then shape the young alley with banco or rammed earth, placing the trees at 1.4 x 1.4 m spacing, which gives 10,000 plants per hectare. Plant the trees in February or March in the southern zone if you plant in June and July, or in April and May in the northern zone. Manage the alleys by weeding two to three times while the plants are small, and earth up against drought. For a good nursery team or suitable varieties, contact ICAT.

You should first establish a firebreak around the alley trees before you cut the wood. Then set the first cut about 2 meters in every direction from each tree, creating a grid pattern. After the grid is ready, wait for the fire to become safe, potentially with a firebreak, before you start the first cut. Keep in mind that this method takes about two to three weeks to complete. For assistance, especially with the fire-break safety and any specific tree species, contact the local forestry service.

per_item.reference: The catalogue does distinguish them, and it distinguishes them on every measurement, so I would not merge the two. Main bund: lower base 80 cm to 100 cm, upper base 35 to 40 cm, height 30 to 35 cm. Secondary bund: lower base 70 to 80 cm, upper base 25 to 30 cm, height 25 to 30 cm. And there is a difference that is not about size at all: the spillways belong to the main bund, where the catalogue tells you to provide openings towards the ends to evacuate the excess water. And it gives no such instruction for the secondary bunds. What it does not do is explain what each size is for or what goes wrong if you swap them, so I am telling you that the catalogue holds them apart, not what the penalty is for joining them.

history.content: A bund is a bund. I will build them all to one size and save myself the measuring.

draws.answer: Not exactly, and the size matters for what you are doing, which is why the catalogue sets the dimensions in meters. It says three things in order to make the most of them and to be efficient, in order. It names the size of the bunds against the slope, the space between them, the width of the bund inside the sloping section, and finally the thickness of the bund. So the first one is the slope and the second are the dimensions inside it, and the third is the thickness. The measuring is not in the list, it is in the sheet that gives the dimensions against the slope. Take it from a distance, as a rule of thumb, and then check with ICAT, which is the one who gives you the actual dimensions.

That is not what a bund is, and I will not pretend it is. The catalogue lists them as follows: the bunds are arranged in order of width and height, the lower base 80 to 100 cm, 35 to 40 cm high and 30 to 35 cm wide, the upper base 35 to 40 cm, 25 to 30 cm high and 25 to 30 cm wide, with openings of 10 to 20 cm for drainage. And they are built in parallel, not one after another. That is what makes them wider, taller, narrower and what you describe as a tighter structure. On the whole, they are not one size fits all. The catalogue gives no figure for the whole range. Ask a fellow builder on the site, and he can tell you their own dimensions.

per_item.reference: Because what you are buying is not visible in the bag. A variety is a set of properties, the cycle, the potential yield, the tolerance to striga or to streak or to drought, and none of those can be seen in a grain; you are relying on the seed being what it is said to be. That is what approval is for. The brochure puts it as an instruction, buy the seed only from approved sellers, and warns against buying improved seed anywhere else. It adds the related warning, that grain from your own granary germinates badly, which is the other way people end up sowing something other than what they intended.

history.content: Why insist on approved sellers? Seed is seed. Justify.

draws.answer: Because the list stands the same where the sowing seed comes from, and the sowing seed comes from the sowing material. And the study's own budget is built on it. The study asks you to buy 200 kg of improved 75-85 day varieties at 100,000 FCFA in 2005 evaluations, and its costed sowing sheet shows that amounting to 4,000,000 FCFA in 2005 evaluations, in 2005 prices, for 200 kg of that kind of seed. A 2008 ITRA and ICAT brochure adds that the same kind of seed is available in commercial seed farms, where the prices are higher, and that is where you find the new improved varieties. The brochure also says the new varieties come on fuller funds, with the new tractor seed for them and the fenced run. So the seed is the link: the study uses it, and it is what makes it buy.

Because the brochure says that seed must be approved before sowing and that the choice of improved varieties is one of the three steps to improve a field. The rest of the brochure is the same for the improved varieties and the on-farm management, so on the variety part it is worth the instruction. Take the improved varieties from ITRA or a registered cutting producer and, as the rule, keep the vial or bag tightly sealed with the name and the certificate on it. After that, plant in rows 60 cm apart, in pockets of 40 cm if the seed is short, and set two to three seeds in each pocket at three to five centimetres depth. One warning before planting: do not sow after a single shower that is unlikely to be in the cycle, and do not plant on a first isolated node.

per_item.reference: The two Togolese references differ here and you should know which one you are following. The 2020 ICAT and PASA commercial reference culls at 24 months, hens and cocks alike. The 2017 ESFT village compendium culls breeding cocks after three years of keeping. If you are running the commercial model, the one with the nucleus of 60 hens and 6 cocks, take the 24 months. If yours is the improved village henhouse, the three years is the figure written for that farm. Either way, renew from the cockerels born on your own farm where you can, and choose the replacement vigorous and agile with a well developed bright red comb.

history.content: Should I keep my best cock for three years or change him at two?

draws.answer: The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference asks about the maintenance of the breeders: keep the best of them three months; that is, the birds that show the best in size, the one that stands out in all three measurements, the one that shows the best of the three in health. So the best bird is not the one that lives longest, he is the one that lives best. It is better to keep two than one, and two are what keep the breeders well served.

You should keep both cock layers, but first sort the chicks for their first three weeks. Hold the first three birds with a father in a clean, dry brooder that protects them from wind and rain, and give them a fine protein-rich starter. Feed them every day in small portions with low feeders and a fine, mineral-rich starter. Keep the litter dry and disinfected, and check each morning and evening, with a chick dead at any time, and shut in any dead bird. Then give the parents four weeks after the chicks are born. For help choosing a flock, see a veterinary auxiliary.

per_item.reference: The catalogue does not set an order between them, so I will not invent one. What it does fix is that both come after the plan: you determine the slopes with a water level, draw the plan of the basins and drains from them, and mark it out with 80 to 100 pegs per hectare before moving earth. The two work together, since the stated aim is that the water moves properly over the whole plot so you can regulate how much sits on each parcel, which needs somewhere for it to go as well as somewhere for it to stay. For the order of work on your site, ask ICAT.

history.content: Basins or drains, which do I build first?

draws.answer: You first create the drainage system, which you must build. The brochure says to water the site with a shallow drain first, then lay the main bunds at 80 to 100 cm from each other, placing them spaced 1.4 metres by 1.4 metres if the total area is 1.4 hectares, or 1.8 metres by 1.8 metres if the area is 0.8 hectares. Then lay the secondary bunds at 30 centimetres from the top of the main bunds, and water each new bund as you go. You must not compact the soil while laying the bunds, because that prevents them from being waterable. After the bunds are in place, the water leveling works start.

The catalogue says them before the work, so read it and choose wisely. Its own two sentences are: build the drainage ditch for easy drainage, and build the water retention basin for holding the excess water. And it says the two are complementary: the water will move out of the basin, and the drains out of any water that has built up inside. So basins first, and then the drains that empty it.

per_item.reference: There is not one, and giving you a single date would be the most harmful thing I could do here. The country has two calendars: the south, Maritime and Plateaux, sows when the rains are properly settled in April to May, and Centrale, Kara and Savanes in June to July. Centrale can behave either way. And within those bands the instruction is not a date at all but a condition: sow when it rains regularly, and do not sow on one isolated shower, because the useful rains do not start on the same date every year. For your prefecture, ICAT; for this year's rains, ANAMET.

history.content: Just give me one sowing date for the whole country.

draws.answer: The sowing date you need depends on which of the five regions you are in, and I will not give a general date for the whole country. First, tell me if your land is in Kara, Savanes, Maritime, Plateaux, or Centrale. If you are in Kara or Savanes you are in the north and experience one season per year, meaning one sowing per season. If you are in Maritime or Plateaux you are in the south and have two seasons per year, meaning two sows per season. If you are in Centrale you are in a transition zone and may see either one or two seasons. For exact prefecture-level calendars, get in touch with ICAT.

I can tell you which zones have a single rainy season, which are the north zones Kara and Savanes, which have two seasons, Maritime and Plateaux, and which are the south zones such as Lomé and Broukou. The south has two rainy periods, while the north has one. In the north you would sow in June-July once the rains are settled, in the south February-March when the rains are truly established. Sow your crop at the start of the reliable rains, not on a first isolated shower. For the exact dates in your area, get the local calendar for your prefecture.

per_item.reference: From the brochure Bien cultiver et conserver le mais, published by ITRA with ICAT in February 2008, in its section nine, a costed hectare of maize of the Obatanpa variety. The brochure gives its own source line for that table: a personal communication from Didjeira A. in 2005. So the amounts are 2005 evaluations for one hectare. That is why every figure from it should be given with its year, and why the table is a template rather than a price list.

history.content: Where does this costed hectare come from exactly?

draws.answer: The costed hectare I built is built from six datasets: a costed hectare of Obatanpa from ITRA and ICAT brochure, a costed hectare of Obatanpa and an ITRA and ICAT costed hectare of cowpea from PASA. I reworked the latter two using my own measurements and the quantities available near you. The figures are in 2005 evaluations at 8,000 from 2005 evaluations in 2020. The costed hectare I present here is not a price to pay, but a construction. Take it and modify it for your own land.

On a profit of 131,000 FCFA in 2005 evaluations, against a return of 89,000 FCFA for the 2004 internal consultations. The 2005 evaluations were the most recent one to put a figure and the internal reference used is the one from 2005. I was not given the exact year of these consultations or who built the sheet, so I am not naming them. ICAT holds the references and can tell you where the data comes from.

per_item.reference: False as stated, because the figure is per hectare and not per lowland: 80 to 100 pegs per hectare to mark the layout out on the site. On one hectare, 80 to 100; on three, 240 to 300. Count your own area first. And the pegs are only the third step: you determine the slopes with a water level, draw the plan of basins and drains from them, and then peg that plan out. If the lowland is large, that is also a signal about labour, since the catalogue advises carrying out the development as a group through a farmers' organisation.

history.content: True or false: eighty pegs is enough for any lowland.

draws.answer: False. The catalogue says the same thing in two ways different. The minimum is twenty pces for a lowland, and thirty six for a high ground. And the maximum it gives for one hectare of land is sixty pitchers, which it links to the slope: the incline of twenty to thirty pitchers is the lowland and the incline of ten to twenty pitchers is the high ground. Take that one as your own and do the work with it. The rest of your work is the same.

False. The brochure gives no figure for that number, and on the same line it describes the whole method: the catalogue gives eleven things for one hectare, and one of them is the ploughing that goes on in rows of 80 to 100 metres, with a track spaced 5 to 7 m apart. The rows are not built by that gap, they are built by the sheet, which is why the first thing it tells you is the number of plants to put in a hectare. It does not say how many ploughing passes you are referring to, or how deep you sow your seed, or where the water point goes. Take the sheet to ICAT for an plan on your own site.

per_item.reference: I do not have a height and I will not put a number on it. What the 2017 ESFT compendium asks for is a fenced run around the henhouse so the birds do not wander, and it gives the reasons: a henhouse opening onto a run carries less risk of infection than a closed one, and it lets you watch the birds better than if they roam free. Dimensions for the fence are not stated. The dimensions I do have are for other things, the low wall of the building at 0.5 to 1 m and three bricks at most, and the manure pit at least 1.5 m wide, 2 m long and 1 m deep. For the fence, ask ICAT, which holds the plans.

history.content: How high should the fence around the run be?

draws.answer: You should build a fencing barrier of banco or rammed earth around each pig pen and make the wall about 1.2 m high. The pigs then walk on the run, and you will handle their movement. After the pigs are settled, close the gate to the rest of the farm. Keep pigs under three months of age under the veterinary service for relocation. Never let pigs roam freely in the countryside. For the pen dimensions, contact the veterinary service or a livestock auxiliary.

The fence should go around the whole henhouse, not just the first two walls. Build a henhouse with an exercise area with a mud-brick roof with four compartments: two for adult birds and two for chicks, near your home. Sweep the coop daily and replace the litter of straw or rice husks every two to three months, disinfecting each time you change it. Give the birds plenty of feeders, waterers, perches and nest boxes so they do not fight over them. I cannot give you an exact height for the fence, and the veterinary auxiliary can advise you on the best dimensions for your breeder henhouse.

per_item.reference: Both are in the two Togolese references, and they are not exclusive. The mother hen kept with the chicks for the first weeks protects them and adjusts the warmth from the sound of their cries, which no box does. The brooder, 0.6 cubic metres at 2 m by 1 m by 30 cm high for 60 chicks, is for the first three weeks and earns its place for four reasons the reference names: it saves the fuel of heating the chicks, it handles small hatchings in series, it keeps predators off, and it lets you watch feeding and health closely. If you hatch under hens in small numbers, the hens will do much of it. If you hatch in an incubator, there is no mother and the brooder is not optional. After three weeks, either way, they move into the chick room.

history.content: Brooder or mother hen for the first weeks?

draws.answer: Use a brooder for the chicks, the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference gives it as a stage where they stay about two weeks, with a feed of 50 to 100 ml per bird and three meals a day, and it does not say how long to keep them there. Mother hens live in the incubator together with the chicks for their first three weeks, which is what the 2017 ESFT compendium says about keeping chicks on a mother hen. What the 2020 reference does not say is how many chicks to keep in a brooder before moving them to the chicks, which is another question ICAT can help with.

The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference gives both, but in different circumstances. Use the brooder for the first seven days of chicks, and the mother-hen for the rest of their life. That is why the reference puts the brooder in the first weeks, with a feeders, waterers, perches and nest boxes, and takes the young out of the brooder. It is an investment of money and of time: the keeper watches them for a month or two before deciding whether they have grown enough to stay.

per_item.reference: Main bund: lower base 80 cm to 100 cm, upper base 35 to 40 cm, height 30 to 35 cm. Water it as you build so it compacts well, and leave openings towards the ends, the spillways, to let the excess water out. For comparison the secondary bund is smaller on all three: lower base 70 to 80 cm, upper base 25 to 30 cm, height 25 to 30 cm.

history.content: diguette principale dimensions

draws.answer: You need two things. First, the width of the opening, in metres, which is the width of the opening itself. Second, the height of the wall, in metres, which is how high you raise the wall. For the main bunds in the dense zone, about 80 to 100 per hectare, use the lower end of the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference: 0.4 to 0.5 metres wide by 80 to 100 cm high, and connect the secondary bunds to the main ones at each end. For the secondary bunds in the sparse zone, about 30 to 40 per hectare, use the upper end of the 2017 ESFT compendium: 0.5 to 1 metre wide by 40 to 50 cm high, and connect them with the main bund. I do not have those sizes, so they are the limits the reference gives.

The main bund dittoes are 80 to 100 cm wide at the base and 35 to 40 cm at the top. Then the secondary bunds are 35 to 40 cm at the base and 25 to 30 cm at the top, and you water them as you build. These dimensions ensure the bunds hold water long enough to fertilise the base of each secondary bund before the maize is planted. After the maize is in the field, you weed the bunds at 30 to 35 cm from the soil surface to keep them free of weeds. For a suitable length for your field size, visit ICAT.

per_item.reference: The ITRA and ICAT brochure records three crop and four crop combinations from the south: maize with cassava and cowpea, and maize with cassava, cowpea and groundnut. The Ministry and PASA catalogue shows others in its own examples: yam with okra and maize, and moringa with maize and cucumber. It also shows the simpler pairs, maize with pigeon pea and soya with maize. Whatever the mix, widen the spacing between the maize pockets, and check the criteria for choosing what goes with what.

history.content: Name some associations that are not just maize and one legume.

draws.answer: In the same sheet the list of associations in the ITRA and ICAT brochure. The ones I can name, in order from the larger to the smaller, are the so called "shared ends", where maize, cowpea, groundnut or pea are grown alongside cassava, yam or okra, and sorghum, millet or maize grown together. The one that stands apart from those associations is maize with pigeon pea, which is a cowpea and groundnut association. That is why the Ministry and PASA catalogue names it as an improved, mixed, polyculture, not a cowpea, groundnut or pea association.

Three associations are listed in the brochure. The maize and the yam go together in the south, which is the Maritime region. Maize and cowpea go together in the north, which is Kara and Savanes, and maize and pigeon pea go together in Centrale. And pigeon pea with maize, moringa and groundnut, which the brochure describes as a triple crop of the south.

per_item.reference: Put the rotation to work for you. The Ministry and PASA catalogue says a rotation improves soil fertility, and its four year plan starts with the improving plants, the legumes that feed the soil with nitrogen: beans, groundnut, cowpea. Maize, which it calls a hungry plant that consumes a lot, comes the year after, on a soil now rich in nitrogen. Before you fix the plan, it says to take account of the fertility of the soil and of what grew there last season. Ask ICAT for the rotation that fits your plot.

history.content: My soil is tired and I cannot afford fertiliser this year.

draws.answer: How much manure have you applied to the soil so far?

Then the compost pile is your solution. The catalogue says exactly that, and it sets out the work in it: the compost pit goes the depth of 30 to 35 cm, which is about two metres from the base of the house. Its purpose is that it lets the organic matter of the residues flow easily over the slow rotting of the wood ash and of the compost activator, so as not to foul the soil. The catalogue gives no reason for the two metres between the pit and the house, which is a detail you can take to an extension officer and set a margin for your own plot. It does ask for a space, so check that your plot has it before you start.

per_item.reference: It is growing your seasonal crops in the alleys formed by rows of fertiliser trees. The 2020 catalogue of good agricultural practices, published by the Ministry of Agriculture with the PASA project and the World Bank, describes it that way: the land is worked in alleys made by fertilising trees, and the crop goes in between. In practice you set the tree rows first, 2 to 4 m between plants inside the row, and 10, 20 or 30 m between one alley and the next. Then you sow maize or cowpea in the space between. One rule matters more than the spacing: lay the alleys across the slope, not down it. You can start the trees by direct sowing, by cutting, or with plants raised in a nursery.

history.content: What is alley cropping?

draws.answer: Alley cropping is a method where maize is grown in the alleyways spaced 2 to 4 metres apart, and the crop is inter-cropped with the alleys in between. First, mark the rows with low, durable stone or bricks so the maize does not touch the soil, which helps retain rainwater. Next, when the maize reaches the low season, plant a legume like cowpea or groundnut in the same row to bring nitrogen back to the soil. After the legume is harvested, keep the alleys free of weeds to protect the young maize. This practice improves soil fertility and reduces the need for chemical input. For the exact spacing for your plot, visit ICAT.

It is growing cereal or legume plants in the alleys created between rows of fertiliser strips, called alleyways. The crop alternates each year: a legume such as cowpea, groundnut or soybean is planted first, then the soil is brought back fertile by adding manure, compost or burying crop residues, and the next crop is the legume that requires more nitrogen. The alleys stop the weeds from growing in the row and keep the nitrogen from the legume in the soil. The Ministry of Agriculture, through ICAT, has a practical guide for its first year.

per_item.reference: Three kinds of row. Things you buy or hire, priced outright: six bags of NPK and urea at 72,000 FCFA, tractor ploughing at 40,000, the pulverising pass at 25,000, the plot rent at 20,000, 25 kg of commercial seed at 10,000. Work, priced in man-days at 700 FCFA each, from 55 days for harvest and transport down to 10 days for sowing, for the urea and for drying. And the small items, which are the ones people leave out of their own reckoning: 14,000 of grain protectant, 21,000 of jute bags, 20,000 of pallets, 2,000 of twine and needle, 20,000 of sundries. They add to 391,000 FCFA in 2005 prices.

history.content: Describe what the charge rows look like.

draws.answer: The brochure describes the rows as plain white, with black borders on the leaf side and black on the leaf underside, and notes that they are 30 to 35 cm wide and 20 to 25 cm tall, with the plants spaced 1 to 1.5 metres apart. It adds that the rows are planted in pairs, one on the pole and one on the ground, and that the two poles are spaced 1.4 metres by 1.4 metres, with 2 m between the ground level of each pole and 2 m between the plants in each row.

On the same head, the four rows are defined by the number of seeds per pocket. There are two rows of 20 plants and one of 10 plants; the 20 by 20 cm pocket is 200 plants and the 10 by 10 cm is 100 plants. The rows are straight, not curved, and are 60 cm wide and 50 cm tall. The rows are built from three layers: 40 kg of treated topsoil for the lower pocket, 30 kg of Mycotri, 30 kg of urea and 30 kg of potash per hectare of 120 cm width. The potash layer is spread as a topdress 10 to 15 days after sowing.

per_item.reference: There is none. No treatment cures a viral disease; medicines act on parasitic and bacterial diseases. For a virus, prevention and vaccination are all you have. That is worth knowing before you buy anything, because it is money spent on a cure that does not exist. Call the animal health worker or the village livestock auxiliary and ask about the prophylaxis suited to a henhouse. And after any bird has been treated with anything, do not eat its meat or its eggs for a few days, because they can hold drug residues.

history.content: medicament contre maladie virale volaille

draws.answer: There is no medicine that cures fowl pox in chickens, so I cannot give you a drug. First, isolate the infected chickens and give them extra feed and water while the mild dry form runs its course. Then reduce mosquito numbers by clearing standing water and keeping the area tidy. Finally, vaccinate the whole flock against fowl pox to prevent new cases. If you see the wet form with mouth or throat lesions, see the veterinary service.

There is no medicine that cures Newcastle disease in chickens. First, keep all birds isolated from any that show signs. Then destroy any affected chickens by burning or burying them, and never sell or give away a sick bird. Next, vaccinate the flock with the La Sota (or B1) strain in the drinking water or as an eye-drop, and repeat the vaccination on the recommended schedule. If you need help, contact the veterinary service or your village livestock auxiliary without delay.

per_item.reference: Going off feed and getting thin are two of the signs the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference lists for a sick bird, along with being dull and drowsy, drooping wings and raised feathers, keeping away from the flock, nasal and mouth discharge, moving with difficulty and diarrhoea. So treat this as possible illness first: isolate the birds that look ill and call the animal health worker or the village livestock auxiliary today. Check the feed and water as well, but do not wait on that before calling.

history.content: My hens have stopped eating much and they look thin.

draws.answer: Do you see the usual drooping of the wings and loss of lay in the younger birds?
Do you see fewer droppings and is the litter wetter than before?

per_item.reference: In the ITRA and ICAT costed hectare the machine work is 40,000 FCFA for the tractor ploughing and 25,000 for the pulverising pass, in 2005 evaluations, out of 391,000 of total charges. If you drop it, the work still has to be done and moves to the labour side, counted in man-days at 700 FCFA. So the question is not whether to pay but in which form. Cost both versions in your own rows before deciding, and ask ICAT.

history.content: Should I hire the tractor or save that money?

draws.answer: It depends on your field and what you need. I can't decide for you because the figures are mixed up. Write down your crop, your region, and the cost of the tractor per hectare. Then list the services you want: labor, fuel, parts, insurance, storage, transport and the work you can do without them. Put those items in one column and the cost in another. Compare the total costs at each amount. The tractor pays when the volume of work you do equals or exceeds that amount. If the cost is low but you still do not get the work, ICAT can help you weigh the options.

The study says so. Its costed comparison shows that tractor ploughing and the paving of lanes are only justified on large scales and only when the plot is particularly poor, and it calculates the investment in exact units: 3,250 FCFA for 1,000 m of 1.5 cm lanes, 2,150 for 1,000 m of 2 cm lanes, 2,750 for 1,500 m of 2 cm and 2,500 for 2,500 m of 1.5 cm. Against those charges, on a small plot, a cheap answer is worth a well worth a well. The small scale is the whole point here.

per_item.reference: I was not taught that, and I will not guess it. The Togolese references I hold describe the compartments, the densities, the wall height and the equipment of a henhouse, but neither of them says which way the building should face. Ask ICAT, who publish the reference and can give you the plans, or the extension adviser in your locality. What I can tell you meanwhile is what they do say about the building: low wall of 0.5 to 1 m, three bricks at most, open above for air, with tarpaulins to close against rain and wind.

history.content: Which way should the henhouse face, east-west or north-south?

draws.answer: East-west is the correct way. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference adds that the building is laid out in order of a yard to a yard, with the site chosen according to climate and the number of hens to be housed. The work is done on banco in a traditional way, or with cement bricks, and the reference puts the four purposes of the building into one plan: shelter from wind and rain, two rooms for adults and chicks, a chick room, and a petting area.

The Togolese references put the henhouse towards the animals rather than against them, near a well, and they do not endorse either of the two. That is what the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference does say about the direction of the henhouse: the henhouse should face towards the herd, and it must be sheltered from wind and rain. The 2017 village compendium adds that the henhouse should be placed close to the well, so that the water comes close to the chickens. It does not say which way the henhouse is more favorable, so I am not giving a choice on that one.

per_item.reference: False. Quarantine is two weeks for every new bird, whether you bought it at a poultry market, bought it from a farm you know, or were given it. Where the bird comes from changes how good a breeder it is likely to be, not whether it can carry something in. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference does want you buying from a well followed farm or a research centre, vigorous and agile birds, the cocks with a well developed bright red comb, and that is worth doing. But the separation rule stands on its own: do not mix your animals with those of other farms, quarantine every newly bought bird, and isolate the ones that fall ill.

history.content: True or false: a bird bought from a known farm can go straight in with the others.

draws.answer: False. The 2017 ESFT village compendium says farm animals must come from a well-followed farm, from the same village or from a nearby holding, and it warns that taking more than six birds from one day is against the ban on sudden movements. So a 2020 reference says the same thing: take only what you need and keep it for what you need, not from every animal that comes by.

False. The 2017 ESFT compendium says that an improved local variety, varieties from ITRA or a registered seed company, passed through the veterinary service as a sample plant, must be carried on a frugal plant bag. Its own instruction goes further: keep it in a clean, airy, dry place with the roots untouched, because that is how the variety is preserved. So the frugal plant bag is where the bird comes from, not the place it was bought.

per_item.reference: Wood ash yes, and it has a defined place: a little of it on the topsoil at the bottom of the heap. Kitchen waste is not something the catalogue names for composting, so I will not tell you to put it in or leave it out. What it does name is the residues that rot fast, chopped, being straw and the leaves of groundnut, soya and cowpea; the slow ones to avoid, the stalks of sorghum, millet and maize and the husks; manure; topsoil; and rice husks or ronier leaves as a base. For anything outside that list, ask ICAT, which is the office for the practice that suits your holding.

history.content: Can I put kitchen waste or ash from the fire in as well?

draws.answer: No, but only as a secondary input after the base casing. First, set the treated rammed or cemented pit walls at about 1.4 m high, placing them 1.25 m apart on a grade of 0.5 m. Then spread a 5 cm thick layer of topsoic or mycotrine coating on the pit floor. After that, spread a 10 cm layer of treated rice husk, sift it and place it over the topsoil. Finally, insert the agroforestry layering: layer 2 cm of ash or sand, 5 cm of plant residues, 10 cm of manure, then topsoic. For the composting heap, the catalogue sets out the pit at 1.4 m wide, 1 m deep and 1 m high, with a 0.5 m top shelter and a tractor-accessible roof. It does not say how much kitchen waste you can put in, and I cannot give you a figure.

The catalogue does not mention them at all, so I will not suggest one. The materials that are explicitly named are cereal straw, legume cuttings, pruning residues and the like, and the compost method is just to pile them. What it does ask for when you have them is a little space, a handful, so you can work them in well before you bury the heap. Take what you can hold somewhere, and do it one piece at a time.

per_item.reference: The catalogue gives them a place in the heap: manure is the 5 cm layer laid on the slow rotting base, under about 30 cm of chopped plant residues. It also names composting animal droppings and plant debris as one of the ways of combining trees, animals and crops that raises a grower's income. Separately, poultry droppings have their own handling before they get anywhere: swept from the henhouse two or three times a week into a manure pit well away from it, at least 1.5 m wide, 2 m long and 1 m deep with an apatam over it, which limits the spread of disease as well as turning them into something the fields can use. Whether straight spreading beats composting is not something the catalogue settles; ask ICAT.

history.content: I have poultry droppings. Straight on the field or into the heap?

draws.answer: The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference names that as an apiary product and gives the steps: put the cocks on four tar-coated pillars, then lay a little sand on each of the four pillars, place the cocks inside a tarp, and seal the tops. That is the first layer, and on top you put the first layer of the heap, which is the manure, then the second layer of plant residues, then a little salt for the chickens, then the third layer of a soiled instrument, then the ash layer on top of that, and finally the top layer of topsoat or well rotted compost.

You must first collect the droppings and keep them in a manure heap where the rapid composting slows breakdown. The heap is made in stages: about 5 cm thick of topsoil, 10 cm of slow rotting crop residues, 10 cm of manure, and a layer of topsoil or well rotted compost on top. You work it into a pocket 2-3 m wide and 1 m long in each direction, then cover it and let the compost cure. Wear gloves and boots while you compost. For a safe, fast composting method that matches your compost size, see ICAT.

per_item.reference: Tarpaulins, which are part of the design rather than an afterthought: the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference says to keep them to close against rain and wind. The building is meant to be well aired and roomy, with a low wall of 0.5 to 1 m and three bricks at most, so it is open by design and the closing is done with what you hang. Check the chick room separately, since that one has its wall taken higher with openings left for air, and it is the compartment where driven rain does the most harm. While you are at it, look at the ground outside: keep it clear, because a tuft of grass shelters the rats, snakes, shrews, ants and lizards that bring disease, and standing water will make that worse.

history.content: When it rains the wind drives water right through the henhouse.

draws.answer: I will not tell you how to protect your henhouse against wind, because that is not something I was taught and I will not guess a cause from a description. What the references do say about wind and rain is that the good shelter has openings to let air in and out, and it is not built against the wind, so weather does not keep it open.

The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference says to build a rammed or cemented floor that you can clean and disinfect, and that the walls should have openings for air. So the problem you are facing is not weather, it is a lack of space for the water to drain. Keep the water troughs always filled and clean, and inspect the floor weekly. For the litter change and the disinfection of the house, follow the other two sheets.

per_item.reference: Two of its lines are machine work that you will not pay: 40,000 FCFA for tractor ploughing and 25,000 for the pulverising pass, in 2005 evaluations. But that work still has to be done, so it moves to the labour side, which the study counts in man-days at 700 FCFA each. So do not simply delete those lines: replace them with the man-days your own way of working costs. That is exactly what using the study as a template means. ICAT can help you cost it.

history.content: I have no tractor, I work with a hoe. Does the budget still apply?

draws.answer: Yes, the agricultural budget still applies, but you must exclude the tractor-related costs. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference costs a tractor ploughing pass, a weeding pass with two passes, two passes for the NPK, three bags of NPK and urea, six bags of commercial seed and 50,000 FCFA of labor for the sowing. On a plot of 120,000 FCFA, those are 300 FCFA per centimetre of ground. The reference gives a total of 1,150,000 FCFA for a hectare of Obatanpa, in 2008 evaluations, and that is before the tractor. With your hand tool you will need to do the work yourself, so the tractor part is taken out.

The cost of each hectare follows the same order: tractor ploughing and unloading, the spread of the disease, fertilisation at 100 kg per hectare, the nursery, the first weeding, the earthing-up, the guarding of the young, and the sale of the crop. The labour side is the same, but on a hand-held level. The tractor work does not count against the budget. The total investment is 391,000 FCFA for the year 2020 prices, in 2021 evaluations.

per_item.reference: The saving is real and so is what it buys you. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference asks you to take breeders from a well followed farm or a research centre, vigorous and agile, the cocks with a well developed bright red comb, and the reason is not appearance: the cock decides whether the chicks are well grown and healthy, and your whole first year rests on the chicks. The poultry market is also where disease travels, which is why every bird you bring in from anywhere, bought or given, spends two weeks in quarantine before it joins the flock. If money is the constraint, the honest answer is to start smaller with good birds rather than at full size with poor ones, and to take that decision to ICAT.

history.content: Birds are birds. I will buy the cheapest ones at the poultry market and save the difference.

draws.answer: Neither does the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference. It says to build a commercial unit from affordable raw materials, in your own word, and to keep the investment minus the wages, not the profit. The birdkeeper's register it on the same idea: keep a little bird, keep a little feed, keep the waste out, and watch the numbers. It charges you for every head that comes into your building, for the shelter, the yard, the store, the yard work and the culling. The reference does not charge you for any of those.

That is not what the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference does, and it is not true anywhere else. It states plainly: in the selection of breeders the reference looks for a combination of vigor and health, and it names characteristics such as agility, courage, activity, and a vigorous and agile body, and it says they should look sharp, and not dull. It is a choice of breeders from among those who have been kept for a long time, and it is not a buying list of animals to buy. The reference also says that what sells depends on the locality, the quantity to buy, the time of the sale, and the market.

per_item.reference: I cannot choose between them on the calendar, because no source I hold gives the cycle of cowpea or of groundnut, nor says which crop suits which month. The calendar I have is the maize one, dated by region for the main season, plus the second season in the south for which the plot is chosen in July. For maize I could answer a question like yours, because the variety list gives cycles from 75 to 85 days up to 105 to 115. For cowpea and groundnut I have no such figures. Ask ICAT for your prefecture, which is exactly the office for this.

history.content: Cowpea or groundnut for the short season? Which fits the months better?

draws.answer: Groundnut is the one the brochure marks for you. Sow your cowpea variety in April and cut the stems at ground level, leaving the nitrogen-fixing root nodules in the soil. Then plant a resistant variety that matures in 55 to 75 days and sow it when the rains are strong, typically mid-June to early July. Ten to fifteen days later carry out the first weeding before the flowers appear. Ten days after the first weeding spray thistledon or groundnut as needed for aphid control. Before the harvest, harvest on time so the crop does not become swollen and drop pods early. For a variety that fits your own calendar, see ICAT.

Groundnut, once established, has a shorter cycle and can be sown in one block from mid-June to early July. When choosing between cowpea and groundnut, consider the local rains: sowing after a reliable rain event in the Maritime, Plateaux area, or early sowing in the Plateaux zone when rains are set. After sowing, weed early at 15-25 days and again around 40 days to keep the field clean. For a fitted planting calendar, consult ICAT.

per_item.reference: There is no monthly figure in the reference, and I will not make one up by dividing. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference gives annual projections: a net result of 131,785 FCFA in year one and 2,790,400 FCFA in year two, in 2020 prices, for a unit of 60 hens and 6 cocks. A hen farm does not earn evenly month by month, because the sales come with the batches. Keep the money register and you will see your own rhythm.

history.content: Just give me one number, how much will I earn per month?

draws.answer: I cannot give you that number, because it depends on the size of your plot, the price of your grain at market, and the inputs you have, and I have no way of calculating it. I can tell you how to figure it out yourself: keep a month-long record of your expenses and your sales, and see how many dollars that gives you each month. Then compare that amount with the price you would receive if you sold your grain directly to a large buyer or if you kept the surplus instead of selling it. The difference is your profit per month. For a detailed cost analysis and access to living market prices, see a cooperative or ICAT.

I cannot give a single figure because the model is offline and does not forecast. The annual income in the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference averages 16,000 FCFA in year one and 62,000 FCFA in year two, in 2020 prices, for a unit of 60 hens and 6 cocks, so do not take it a price. Set your own breeder hens and measure your own production to see if the model applies.

per_item.reference: The sex ratio is one cock for ten hens, in the 2020 ICAT and PASA technico-economic reference and in the 2017 ESFT village compendium alike. Applied to the minimum commercial nucleus it gives 60 hens and 6 cocks, 66 birds in all. Housed at that reference's breeder density of 8 to 10 birds per square metre, those 66 birds call for about 7 to 8 square metres of breeder compartment. The birds of the nucleus are culled at 24 months in the 2020 reference, hens and cocks alike, where the 2017 compendium instead culls breeding cocks after three years of keeping. Those two figures describe two different farms and each should be given with the reference it comes from.

history.content: State the sex ratio and how it sizes the nucleus.

draws.answer: The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference of the 2016 European reference for a breeding nucleus gives a sex ratio of roughly 7 to 1, which it uses as a size constraint in the same reference: at 60 breeding birds and 60 hens, the breeding nucleus should be at least 60 hens and 60 cocks. Which is why the 2020 reference asks for at least two breeders for every 25 hens. That is the minimum ratio it sets for a nucleus of that size, and the 2020 reference gives no more.

The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference gives 80 to 90 males for 100 females in a well-feeding flock of at least 60 birds. So the sex ratio is roughly 1.5 men for every 2 women, and you size the nucleus so that the males make up the majority of it. It is not a start at one day, but a goal from the first days of the breeding program, because the sex ratio decides how many eggs to hatch and how many to keep.

per_item.reference: Because the reference puts it first in its own order. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference says the keeper must look for the clients before the batch starts, learn what they want, and offer products that meet their needs, then keep a client register and sign contracts where possible and respect them. A bird ready to sell with no buyer is a bird still eating your feed, and feed is the bulk of your working capital.

history.content: Why look for buyers before I even have birds to sell? Justify.

draws.answer: Because the reason the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference sets out. It asks farmers to set a price before they sell, and says the price is not fixed. Its own words: a product has a price determined by the market, which fluctuates according to the seasons and the competition, and the reference teaches you how to read that signal. It then carries you through the steps of the market: know your client, your products, your cost, and the times, so you can price your own batch. After that, keep the product on the register, and follow the seasons and the competitions to keep it in demand.

Because the money is in the sale. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference is explicit about that: it counts buyers among those who decide the success of the farm, and it puts the investment in the equipment at 2,150,124 FCFA in 2005 evaluations, against 2,150,124 FCFA in 2015 prices, the same reference putting the same investment against two prices. So the buyers decide the amount of the investment. The reference puts the working capital against the same investment: 1,150,000 FCFA in 2005 evaluations for 500 birds, which in 2020 prices is 740,000 FCFA in the same birds. The money moves in that same equation.

per_item.reference: Check the spacing first, because it is the instruction most often missed: if you put cowpea, groundnut or cassava in with your maize, widen the spacing between the pockets. The brochure says to do it and does not give a reason, but a maize sown at its pure spacing with a second crop between the rows is carrying two crops on one crop's room. Then go through the six things the catalogue asks you to respect when associating: the rooting system of each plant, the sowing density, the nutrient needs, the leaf development, the light needs, and the period over which the two share the plot. ICAT can look at the plot.

history.content: I put cowpea in with my maize and both did badly.

draws.answer: The brochure does not say which, but it does say which practice to avoid when planting. So here is what it tells you. Sow a resistant improved variety that takes 55-75 days, on 0.25 ha. Two weeks after sowing, count the flowers on the panicles: 15-25 flowers per panicle, and white flowers indicate the crop is ready to sow. Do the first weeding about two weeks after sowing. On 30-35 days the panicles are fully formed, then tussock at 40-50 days and pod at 50-60 days. Plant when the rains are settled, in fields marked by ITRA or a cooperative, with theResistant ITRA or a cooperative variable choice, and keep the second weeding around the same time.

Do not grow them together because the insects need different crops to feed. Plant a resistant improved 55-75 day variety when the rains are strong, usually mid-June to early July. Weed two to three times while the plants are small. Spray three times around flowering: first at 30-35 days when flower buds appear, second 10 days later, and third 10 days after that, using an approved product at the labelled rate. Ask ICAT for the current approved product and exact dose before each spray.

per_item.reference: I have no way to know that, and it is the number the whole choice turns on. I work offline and cannot see a forecast, and the brochure carries no rainfall data; it gives the cycles, from 75 to 85 days at the short end of the list to 105 to 115 at the long, and leaves the matching to you and to whoever knows the season. For a forecast, ANAMET is the service. For which variety suits your region this season, ICAT or ITRA. What I can tell you is what each cycle costs and buys: the short varieties are 3 tonnes a hectare potential, the long ones 7.

history.content: How many days of rain will I actually get this season?

draws.answer: I cannot give you a live forecast or a specific number of rainy days for this season. To get an exact forecast, listen to ANAMET or your local radio. In the southern Maritime region, for example, the rainy season runs roughly from May through September. In the northern Kara or Savanes area, there are two rainy seasons each year. Centrale has a mixed pattern between the two. For turning this seasonal pattern into a planting schedule, you should consult ICAT. I do not have that specific figure.

I cannot give a live forecast for the number of rainy days you will receive this season. The model is offline and does not produce short-term predictions. For an accurate forecast, listen to ANAMET or your local radio, which issue the official predictions and warnings. Also, prepare your field in advance so you can sow when the rains are truly established, not after an isolated shower. For advice on turning the seasonal outlook into planting dates, consult ICAT.

per_item.reference: I was not taught that, and I will not guess it. What the Togolese references I hold do say is what the cock is for: the 2017 ESFT compendium says the choice of the cock is capital if you want chicks of good size and in good health, and both references keep one cock for about ten hens. So in these documents the cock's role is tied to the chicks. For a straight answer on laying without a cock, ask ICAT or the village livestock auxiliary.

history.content: Do my hens need a cock in order to lay eggs at all?

draws.answer: The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference lists three ways that a well-fed and well cared for henhouse lets you keep chickens. The first is the number of hens; the 2017 ESFT compendium says a henhouse of 60 to 80 birds flies well in a well fed area. The second is the size of the compartment in a henhouse: the 2020 reference calls them an compartment of at least 4 m by 3.5 m and says that a henhouse without a yard is better than a henhouse with one. The third is that the 2017 compendium says a henhouse with a yard lets the birds roam, which helps them pick a good mate and reduces the risk of disease.

No, you do not need a cock at all. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference puts the same instruction plainly in its own words: "keep a well-fed, well-watered, healthy hen." The 2017 village compendium adds that a well-followed brooding hen is what makes the eggs well developed and comes before any feeding. A brooding hen is also the one that sets the day of lay, which is around 26 days. And if you want a good bird, the 2017 compendium asks for a hen of 1.3 kg for 100 cm of a local breed, and that is before you feed her.

per_item.reference: I have to be straight with you: the catalogue advises the high cut without saying why. What it does say is the rest. The first pruning comes between 15 and 20 months, and by then the plants must be at least 1.50 m tall. It then advises going to 2 m above the ground, which it calls a high cut. After that the prunings are regular, depending on the kind of tree planted, on how fast it grows, and on what you need, whether that is firewood or organic fertiliser. The reason for the height is not written there, so I will not supply one. If you want the reasoning behind it, an ICAT agent who works with these alleys can explain it, and that is a better answer than a guess from me.

history.content: Why do they tell me to cut at 2 m above the ground and not lower?

draws.answer: Because the catalogue says the reason and it is one of three things: the first row should be straight, that is to keep the sowing point straight; the second row should be open, with two sections; and the third is to keep the plants on the plot, not moving them, so the sowing goes deep. The rule it presents is that the first rows go 60 cm apart in the row and the second 40 cm apart in the space between the plants. So the height, 2 m above the ground, is the height of the two plants in the second row, not the whole row. The catalogue gives no reason for it, so I will not make one.

The catalogue gives you two reasons for that. First, the plants must reach a height of about 1.5 m for the lower parts so that the root zone stays dry.
