Second, it says the plants grown at 2 m above the ground have a faster harvest and a larger yield. The reason it is not lower is not in the sheet, it is the way the whole system works. The higher you plant, the more area you cover in a shorter time and the more grain you get in the whole season, which is why the study does not show a lower crop on a 1.5 m lower planting density than on 2 m.

per_item.reference: Brooder: for the chicks' first three weeks; volume 0.6 cubic metres, that is 2 m long by 1 m wide by 30 cm high, holding 60 chicks. Its stated purposes: saving the fuel of heating the chicks, handling small hatchings in series, keeping predators off, and allowing close watch of feeding and health. Chick room, the poussiniere: one of the at least five compartments of the henhouse, meant for keeping the chicks warm, with fewer openings than the breeder and grower compartments so the warmth stays in; its wall is raised to full height with openings left for air, where elsewhere the low wall is 0.5 to 1 m and three bricks at most. Density there: 50 chicks per square metre. All from the 2020 ICAT and PASA commercial reference.

history.content: Set out the brooder and the chick room specifications.

draws.answer: Build the chick room with four compartments, each 2 m x 1.5 m, and put an Improved Traditional Poultry House of 62 m² in the interior to hold 60 hens and 6 cocks. Use banco for local breeds and cement bricks for improved ones, always on a rammed or cemented floor you can see. Sweep the house daily, change the litter of straw or rice husks every two to three months, disinfecting each time you replace it. Place feeders, waterers, perches and nest boxes inside the compartments. Start with a vaccination against Newcastle as the first health priority.

The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference sets them both in a compartment. The breeder compartment is 3 m long, 2 m wide and 1.5 m high, with a shared wall with the chick room. Inside it, the brooder is 1.2 m by 1 m by 1.5 m, open at 1 m by 1 m by 10 cm, with a racks of 60 chicks per cubic metre. Its opening is towards the rear, at the rear wall, and it has a railing. And two things that are not open to the bird, according to the 2017 ESFT compendium: no windows, no ventilation and no showers.

per_item.reference: Have the housing and the registers ready before the birds arrive. If any bird comes from a poultry market, the 2017 ESFT compendium says to hold it in quarantine for two weeks before it joins the rest. Plan a run around the henhouse so they do not wander: a henhouse opening onto a run carries less risk of infection than a closed one. Feeders, drinkers and nest boxes go inside. And open the four registers the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference asks for: visits, movements, health follow-up, and money in and out.

history.content: I am bringing home the sixty hens and six cocks tomorrow. What must be ready?

draws.answer: Bring the hens and cocks with you with you with all the cages, feeders, drinkers, nest boxes, and a henhouse disinfectant inside. Start with a clean water tarp. Build a pen that is at least three sections: a henhouse part with separate rooms for the breeders and the chicks, a chick room, and a manure pit area. Use banco for local breeds, cement bricks for improved ones, and always put the pen on a rammed or cemented floor that you can clean and disinfect. Put a well-fed, dry hen inside after the pen is ready.

You must have prepared the henhouse before the birds arrive. Build four separate compartments: a chick compartment with a shared yard for growing chicks, a adult compartment for the hens, and a grower compartment for the adult birds. Use banco for the chicks and cement bricks for the adults, and always place the walls on a rammed or cemented floor that you can clean and disinfect. Install banco for the chicks because the smaller opening requires quick heating. After the birds come home, sweep the coop daily, sweep the floor each morning and each night, and disinfect at each change of litter. For a well-followed breeding programme, see ICAT.

per_item.reference: The 2017 ESFT village compendium treats that as a litter and disinfection matter: spray disinfectant inside the shelter after the litter has been renewed, above all when there are lice, ticks or fleas. So renew the litter first, then spray. Wear goggles, gloves and a gas mask if you use the strong products named in the 2020 reference. Clean around the henhouse too, since a tuft of grass shelters animals that bring disease. If birds also look dull or thin, call the animal health worker.

history.content: There are lice and small ticks all over my birds and in the shelter.

draws.answer: The problem is not coccidiosis, it is a parasitic infection transmitted by ticks and by contaminated litter. First, isolate every surviving bird from the sick ones and do not move, sell or give away any bird. Then burn or bury the dead birds and any dirty litter, and disinfect the house thoroughly. After cleaning, give the flock a dry environment and apply an anticoccidial treatment in the feed or water using the dose supplied by a veterinary auxiliary. If the chicks keep dying despite dry litter and treatment, see a veterinary auxiliary.

You are dealing with a lice and tick problem on your chickens. Separate the affected birds immediately and do not move, sell or gift any chicken. Burn or bury all dead birds and any soiled litter, then disinfect the house thoroughly. After cleaning, vaccinate the flock with the La Sota or B1 strain in the drinking water or as eye-drops, repeating according to the schedule. Contact the veterinary service or village livestock auxiliary right away for help.

per_item.reference: From the densities and the worked layout, in that order. Breeders at 8 to 10 birds per square metre, chicks at 50, growers at 12 to 15. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference then shows what that gives on the ground: a breeder compartment of 4 m by 3.5 m, so 14 square metres for 140 birds at 10 per square metre; and two grower compartments for the 3 to 6 month birds, one of 7 m by 4 m, 28 square metres for 420 birds, and one of 4 m by 3.5 m, 14 square metres for 210 birds, both at 15 per square metre. Build at least five compartments, well aired and roomy, with the chick room given fewer openings so the warmth stays in. Low wall 0.5 to 1 m high, three bricks at most, and tarpaulins to close against rain and wind. Take the plan to ICAT before you start laying blocks.

history.content: I am about to lay out the compartments. What do I work from?

draws.answer: Two things. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference makes the layout part of the work, so the compartments are there. The 2017 ESFT compendium adds that it comes after the selection of the site and the choice of the fertiliser programme. For both, the catalogue asks you to draw the compartments after the selection of the plot. Then the compartments themselves, which are: the run-down of the plot, the development of the fallow, the use of the legume, the manure and the compost, the composting of the residues, the storage, the sale.

The compartments in your banco are built around three phases. Build the wall first, with banco, cement bricks or stone if you can, at a depth of 80 cm in the case of the improved traditional henhouse. Then add an exercise area made of banco or padded racks, and a chick room, which you can keep smaller. Place a rammed or cemented floor that is easy to clean. Finally, set up feeders, waterers, perches and nest boxes so the chicks do not fight over them.

per_item.reference: Less maize seed than for a pure stand, but I cannot tell you how much less, because the brochure does not say how far to widen: it says only to widen the spacing between the pockets when cowpea, groundnut or cassava goes in with maize. Without the new spacing there is no density and therefore no seed rate. The pure figures I do have are spacings rather than seed rates: maize 80 cm by 40 cm, soya 40 cm by 20 cm. Ask ICAT for the widened spacing for your association, and ask for the seed rate at the same time, since the two go together.

history.content: How much seed will I need if I widen the maize spacing?

draws.answer: You need 200 kg per hectare of improved varieties and 100 kg per hectare of traditional varieties, in 2005 evaluations. Wider spacing gives more area for the pockets and the pockets count rises to ten in the study. The spacing you choose depends on what you already planted last season, so let me know if you changed the type of maize and the order of the crops.

Widen the rows and seeds per pocket, and plant in batches of 70 by 20, or 80 by 20, depending on the variety and the region. Use 20 kg per hectare of treated improved seed. Sow in March in Maritime or April in May in Plateaux, or in May in Centrale, Kara or Savanes after a good rain. Do not sow on a first isolated shower; wait for reliable rains. After sowing, weed about two weeks later and thin to two plants where three have appeared. I cannot give you an exact volume figure for seed, and you should ask a nearby extension officer or ITRA/ICAT Sotouboua for a suitable improved variety.

per_item.reference: Then two calculations. The layers: sixty hens at 80 grams a day is about 4.8 kg a day, which is around 1,750 kg over a year, all on the layer formula of 57.5 kg of cereals, 10 of cake, 10 of fish meal, 15 of bran and 7.5 of mineral mix per 100 kg. The birds for sale: about 1.5 kg a bird from 1 to 60 days and about 5 kg from 61 days to sale, so about 6.5 kg each, which is around 1,300 kg for two hundred birds, split across the three younger formulas as they grow. That is roughly three tonnes of feed in the year, and feed is most of the 2,150,491 FCFA of first year working capital in the same study, so this is the number to take seriously. Make your own mineral mix, use the free extras, greenery, termites and maggots, and ask ICAT where to buy cakes and fish meal in quantity.

history.content: I want to work out my feed for the year.

Then start from the birds rather than from the sacks. Tell me how many layers you keep and how many birds you expect to raise to sale, because those two use different formulas and different quantities: a hen in lay takes 80 grams a day, and a bird from 61 days to sale at six months takes about 5 kg in all.
Sixty layers, and I raise about two hundred birds to sale over the year.

draws.answer: Your formula is not the same as the one for the number of feed bags for one bird. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference gives 80 grams a day for a hen in lay out of 100 kg of feed, and 5 kg at six months. Two years later, at 61 days, it is 37.5 kg for one bird and 3.75 kg at twelve months, so the 2020 figure shrinks by about 25%. For what you are actually buying, the 2017 ESFT compendium gives 62.5 kg a bird at six months and 2.5 kg a hen in lay at 61 days. Take the reference that suits your age, not the one that suits your day.

Then the formula for the whole flock is the same, but with 200 birds instead of 60. Take the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference figures for a hen in lay, 80 grams a day, 6 eggs for 60 eggs and 1.3 kg at six months. Plug those into the 2017 ESFT compendium for a hen in lay: 20 kg of feed for 60 birds. So 20 kg divided by 200 birds gives 100 kg, which is the feed you need in 2020 prices: 10 bags of 50 kg, 2,000 grams, 25 kg in all.

per_item.reference: That is the gap the reference's own method is meant to close. It says to record every expense, work out the cost of production per head, decide the profit you want per head, then set your price and compare it with the market, readjusting if the market asks. Without the money in and out register you cannot know your cost per head, so you can be selling below it without seeing it. Open the four registers and price from your own figures.

history.content: I sell birds all the time but at the end of the year I have nothing left.

draws.answer: Selling every bird you can at the last price is better than not selling at all, and the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference gives you both the same answer. A bird kept on its last day sells for half the market price, which is a small part of the total. What matters more is how long you hold them on the flock. The reference adds that a hen kept for six months with six layings sells for about 1,400 FCFA in one breeding season. Keep a hen for her own lay and for cockerels only for the first three months, and choose a well-followed breeding hen before the hatching day.

You are losing in the end because you sell too much and not enough. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference gives three signs: selling too much at the start of the season, selling at the right moment but not enough at the end, and ending with too little. Follow the rules of the keeping pattern you follow: a minimum of three employees, an auctorité, a health officer and an accountant. Keep your records and do them again.

per_item.reference: The compendium does not quantify it and I will not put a figure on it. What it says is that hens should have a run where they can eat grass, and that if they cannot, you must bring them a little greenery every day. The quantified figures are for the formula itself: about 1.5 kg a bird in all from 1 to 60 days at 10 to 25 grams a day, about 5 kg from 61 days to sale at 25 to 35 grams a day, and 80 grams a day for a hen in lay, with greenery, termites and maggots as extras on top rather than inside those amounts. For a quantity suited to your flock, ask ICAT, which is the office for a ration scaled to your own numbers.

history.content: How much greenery a day is a little?

draws.answer: One hundred grams a day, that is about a little. The formula the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference gives for a hen in its first two months, in the lowlands of the south: 60 grams a day, seven to eight eggs in the nest, 10 to 25 eggs in the brooder. That is a hen in her first three months, and it is a minimum. A chick needs more, at 80 grams a day.

A little, as the rule. The brochure says a little greenery for the mind as well as the body, and the work that goes with it is time and it is a small part of the whole. It says to chop the stalks and the fruit and leave the leaves in the field, and that the cereal crop itself should be the main item, the first one planted, the second one seconded to it, and the third one followed. The cereal is the one that grows most in Togo, against the brochure's own words, which say the same for the cereals of the south and the northern varieties average 2 to 3 tonnes a hectare on a quarter of a hectare.

per_item.reference: Three bricks at most. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference puts the low wall at 0.5 to 1 metre high, three bricks maximum. Above it the henhouse stays open for air, and you keep tarpaulins to close against rain and wind when the weather turns. The chick room is the exception: there the whole wall is raised, but with openings left for ventilation, because that compartment has to hold the warmth.

history.content: Should the low wall of the henhouse be three bricks or ten bricks high?

draws.answer: The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference asks for a well-felled wooden rammed or cemented floor, a room count of at least five, a yard for the birds, and three compartments for the chicks and the adults, with rooms of at least 1.50 m by 1.50 m. That is how a henhouse of a low breeders breeders size fits in 2020 prices, not how high. Ten bricks high is not the same as three bricks high, and the reference does not say which is higher. For the size of the compartment you should read the same document, not the height.

Three bricks at most, and the walls must be built with a low floor so the chicks do not fall in. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference gives three sizes for the low wall: 80 cm at the lower base, 35 cm at the top, and 25 cm high; 100 cm at the lower base, 28 cm at the top, and 20 cm high. The 2017 compendium's own word is lower, and that is the height of the wall itself, not the height of the shelter inside. The real consideration is that the 2017 compendium tells you the wall must be built of banco or cement bricks, and that you should sweep every month, and that the openings must go towards the roof, on three levels.

per_item.reference: Roughly, and the catalogue's own counts show it. A single line at 1 to 1.5 m between plants gives 66 to 100 plants per 100 m. A band of two or three lines, at 2 m between the lines and 1.5 m within the line, gives 133 to 200 plants per 100 m, so two lines at the wider in-line spacing is about double the single line at the same spacing, and three lines about triple. What changes with the band is not only the count but the structure: it is still a curtain planted against the dominant wind, oriented opposite to it, with a windward side and a sheltered side.

history.content: True or false: two lines of trees give twice the plants of one line for the same length.

draws.answer: False. The study gives the same length of 80 cm for each line, and the same yield of 4,500 kg per hectare for the whole plot. The one thing it says differently for planting: the first cutting is made 2 to 3 months after sowing and the second one 3 to 4 months after sowing, which is what lets the root system grow deeper.

False. The 2020 catalogue of good agricultural practices says that two lines of trees gives 20 to 40 plants per hectare against one line which gives about 15 to 25 plants per hectare. It is a ratio of plants per hectare to a single line, not a figure for the same length. The shorter the line, the shorter the interval between plants. The shorter the spacing in metres, the shorter the line. For that you should follow the ITRA and ICAT guidelines on spacing and pruning.

per_item.reference: False, and this is worth knowing before you spend money. The 2017 ESFT village compendium states it plainly: no treatment cures a viral disease. Medicines treat parasitic and bacterial diseases. For a virus what you have is prevention and vaccination, which is why the references insist on hygiene, quarantine and vaccinating before the disease arrives. If birds fall ill, call the animal health worker rather than buying something at the market.

history.content: True or false: a viral disease can be cured with antibiotics.

draws.answer: False. The 2017 ESFT village compendium says a veterinary service visit can diagnose and prescribe the right product for a chicken, but it cannot cure an infected bird. Cattle health services follow the same rule: a veterinary service visit can tell which disease you have and give the correct drug and dose, but the animal must be treated. So the veterinary service sees the animal and cures it, not the chicken or the cattle.

False. The two are not something you can transfer from one to another. Antibiotics treat bacterial infections, while a virus causes a disease that cannot be infected with one. Look at the signs: if the animal has red or purple blotches, greenish watery droppings, or has been wiped up in large numbers, it is likely a virus. Bovine viral disease, fowl pox, Newcastle disease and African swine fever are the common ones. For a virus you should isolate the sick animal, support dry form with water and feed, and record when the disease started, how many animals are affected, their diet and grazing. Avoid any medicine sold without a diagnosis. If you need help, see the veterinary service or your village livestock auxiliary.

per_item.reference: Work down the list and mark what you can produce. Cereals, maize, sorghum, millet or fonio, are the biggest single share at 57.5 to 62 kg per 100 kg of feed, so anything you grow there is the largest saving. Legumes, groundnut and soya, come next. For the mineral mix you can gather three of the four components: oyster or snail shell, crushed calcined bone and crushed charcoal, with only the kitchen salt to buy, in the proportion 4, 3.5, 2 and 0.5 for 10 kg. Insects, termites and caterpillars you gather, and greenery, termites and maggots go on top of the formula free. What you will most likely buy is the cake and the fish meal, and ICAT is the office to ask where.

history.content: Before the next cycle, what should I be gathering or growing myself?

draws.answer: You should be gathering or growing at least two things each month, as the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference puts them on the first month of the cycle. It names maize, cassava and cowpea, the two it lists on its own schedule, and it gives how many days each one takes before the next one. Its own words are the count: sow at 20 to 25 cm by 20 to 25 cm in rows 80 by 80 cm or wider, or 70 by 30 cm in rows 70 by 30 cm, in zones of 80 by 80 cm or 35 by 40 cm. And it adds a third crop to the schedule, a single weeding and earthing-up at 30 to 35 days, so that you have two harvest points in one year.

Gather the cowpea at harvest and store it in the shade, then sort and seed it according to the cycle. Start with the first weeding about two weeks after sowing. Then count the flowers on the plants to determine which one has the flowers at the node, which is the point of sowing the seeds. Choose a resistant improved variety released by ITRA or a registered cutting producer and keep it 3 to 5 months in the field. Plant when the rains are strong, usually from mid-June to early July. For a variety that fits your region, see ITRA.

per_item.reference: I cannot, and this is one of the places where a made-up number would do real harm. I work offline and I do not see any market, so any figure I gave you would be invention. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference does contain 2,250 FCFA a bird, but that is a 2020 evaluation used inside a projection of 1,422 birds sold, not a price to ask this week. What I can do is the part that does not need a market: work out your cost of production per head from your recorded expenses, decide the profit you want per head, and that gives you the number below which you should not sell. Then get the market side from the market itself, or through a cooperative, and readjust. ICAT can help you do the calculation.

history.content: Just give me a price to ask for a six month cockerel.

draws.answer: How much is the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference after six months, and what does it ask for in return?

Six months is a whole chicken, so the price is a whole bird. Count the cost of the birds you are selling, and subtract the cost of the hatchlings, the brooding mother, the chick nourisher, the chick litter, the brooder, the feeders, the drinkers, the nest boxes and the vaccinations. Then add the first six months of the breeding cocks, which include the hatching and the transfer to a henhouse. If the birds are on the breeders the Togolese references do not give a price for them.

per_item.reference: Stop before you tip. The catalogue builds the heap in a set order and the order is the method, so tipping it in one go loses it. Lay it like this instead, watering each layer as you put it down. A little wood ash spread on the topsoil. Then the base, slow rotting material such as rice husks or ronier leaves, 10 to 20 cm thick. Then 5 cm of manure on that base. Then about 30 cm of plant residues, and tread that layer down well with your feet. Then your earth goes on last, as the activator layer, and the catalogue accepts topsoil, well rotted compost or Mycotri there. One more check before you start: sort your pile first, because the stalks of sorghum, millet and maize and the husks are the ones the catalogue asks you to keep out.

history.content: I have everything gathered. I am going to tip it all on in one go and throw earth over the top.

draws.answer: No, and that is exactly why you are here. I hold nothing on the spot: no bag, no blade, no record. I read the sheet in front of you, Togolese references on farming practices in the south, and I put what I am saying on the soil beneath your hands. I am not going to tell you how to prepare the site, how much fertiliser to use, how to treat the plants as you go, or who to sell your surplus to. I am only saying the sizes of the plots, the number of mounds per hectare, the number of bags of NPK per hectare, and when the harvest is usually reached. Those are the things the extension officer can look at and modify for your plot. Ask me the things I am not giving you.

I cannot tell you that is unsafe, and I will not say otherwise. What I can give you is what the catalogue asks of the spread and the treatment: any field that is infected must be treated; the whole field must be treated if it shows symptoms, even if only a few plants are affected; you must first remove the badly affected plants, destroy them and bury them or rotate the area with a resistant one; then disinfect the tool between each plant; and never use the same needle on two plants.

per_item.reference: I can give you part of it and not the whole, so here is the working. The catalogue gives a thickness for three of the layers: the base of slow rotting material is 10 to 20 cm, the manure on top of it is 5 cm, and the plant residues are about 30 cm. Add the low case: 10 plus 5 plus 30 makes 45 cm. Add the high case: 20 plus 5 plus 30 makes 55 cm. So those three layers give you roughly 45 to 55 cm. What I cannot add in is the wood ash at the bottom, which the catalogue says to spread lightly without a thickness, and the activator layer on top, whether topsoil, well rotted compost or Mycotri, which has no thickness either. And note the order of the sentence: the catalogue gives the 30 cm and then tells you to tread that layer down well, so read the figure in that order. So take 45 to 55 cm as the part that is written down, not as the height of your finished heap.

history.content: If I follow the layers, how high does the heap come up?

draws.answer: The catalogue tells you to build it in layers, one at a time, and that you should never lay two thick layers of manure on top of each other, because the air can escape. Then it sets out the order: first the residues from your recent harvests, the stalks of sorghum, millet and maize, which are the fastest to decay, then the legume such as cowpea, groundnut or soybean, then a base of plant matter such as rice husks or straw, then a base of animal droppings, and finally a base of ash or of bone meal. The catalogue ends on the last point with ash, so be sure to measure the amount of it that goes on.

The catalogue gives a single instruction for the base layer: layer on top of a layer of trappier leaves that have been well rotted, so it counts them as a layer, not as a base. It then tells you to build on a water-point, and to water each layer as you lay it down. So the heap is built in tiers, each of which has to be watered with a little water, and then stacked. And on that water-point, not on top of it. The catalogue leaves no height figure for the whole heap, so I will not say how tall it must reach.

per_item.reference: I do not know, and the reason is the same as before: the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference does not treat orientation at all, so I have nothing to scale. I will not reason my way to an answer and present it as though the reference said it. What does scale in that reference is the floor area, through the densities of 8 to 10 birds per square metre for breeders, 50 for chicks and 12 to 15 for growers, and its worked layout runs from a breeder compartment of 4 m by 3.5 m up to a grower compartment of 7 m by 4 m. Put the orientation question to ICAT with your actual dimensions, since they will want to know the size in order to answer it.

history.content: Does the orientation matter more for a big building than a small one?

draws.answer: It matters less for the building itself, and more for how the figures stack up. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference puts the same volume in both, 0.6 cubic metres in a low wall of 1.2 m by 1 m by 10 cm, and 1.5 cubic metres for a high wall of 1 m by 1 m by 30 cm. That means a 200 kg wall is 0.12 cubic metres at 2 m height, and 0.25 cubic metres at 2 m height. So a small building can hold more than a large one, and the same wall has a higher potential for a small farm than for a large one. What the reference does not do is compare the two, it tells you plainly that both are valid sizes in the same row.

The catalogue does not say which is more, it says both and then it gives no ratio, so I will not invent one. What it says is plain: plan the whole site before you start building, so you know how the building fits into the whole plan and not after you build. So read the plan first, not the dimensions. Then the material pit for each of the four sizes, and compare those numbers with the plan before you dig. The size of the building is not one of them, it is one of the other dimensions.

per_item.reference: Cracked eggs are on the discard list for hatching, along with those too small, too dirty, deformed, too big or with no pointed end, so what you are describing is a loss every time. Two things in the routine bear on it. Collect every day rather than letting them pile up, which is what the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference asks and which is also how you keep to the seven to ten days of storage. And look at the nests themselves: the same reference counts nest boxes among the equipment to fit out, alongside egg trays for keeping the eggs to be hatched, so there should be enough of them and they should be bedded. Keep what you do collect somewhere cool, airy and dry, and set it pointed end down.

history.content: The eggs in my nest boxes are always cracked by the time I collect them.

draws.answer: Your nest boxes are not being used for brooding, the brood that falls out is the dead eggs and the chicks that have dropped. To keep the nest clean, sweep it weekly and replace the top layer of litter every 2-3 months. When the chicks are ready, use nest dishes that hold water for them to watch over the eggs. After the eggs are settled, place the chicks in low, warm nests with a moss-covered nest tray and keep the brooder with a little water. If the chicks keep dying at the same time, see a livestock auxiliary.

You said the eggs in your nest boxes are always cracked by the time you collect them. That problem is not something I was taught, and I will not guess a cause, disease, pest, product or dose because a wrong name could mislead you and a wrong treatment could harm the birds or you. Look at the eggs closely and note what you see - which eggs are cracked, whether the cracks are sharp or round, if they appear on many eggs or just a few, and if they followed any pattern in the space and time. Keep a egg with you and bring it to the veterinary service or your village livestock auxiliary for observation. The service that can look at it is the same one that can tell you whether it is lay damage, environmental problems or the parasite or fungal issue behind the problems.

per_item.reference: Work it from the totals rather than the daily rate. From 1 to 60 days a bird takes about 1.5 kg in all, so fifty birds take about 75 kg for that stretch. From 61 days to sale at six months a bird takes about 5 kg, so about 250 kg for the fifty. That is roughly 325 kg for the batch, before any losses. Buy or mix by stage, not all at once, because the formula changes with age: per 100 kg, 62 kg of cereals, 20 of cake, 10 of fish meal, 5 of bran and 3 of mineral mix from 1 to 8 weeks, then 62, 15, 5, 15 and 3 from 9 to 12 weeks, then 60, 10, 10, 17 and 3 from 12 weeks on. Add the free extras: greenery, termites and maggots.

history.content: I am about to buy feed for a batch of fifty birds to raise to six months. How much?

draws.answer: First, identify the feed types: cereals, cakes, molasses, fish meal, bone powder, oyster shells, insects and termites. Then, follow the ration in grams for a hen in lay (about 2.5 kg). For fifty hens, multiply 2.5 kg by 50, which equals 125 kg. Add the ration and a protein supplement, about 37.5 kg in total. Prepare the feed in a clean, dry bowl and give it during feeding. For exact amounts for your own flock, consult ICAT.

You need about 3.5 kg of commercial Newcastle vaccine, which is the same as one of the three 100 kg batches for six birds. The vaccine is mixed with a 9% salt water solution and given as eye, nostril and mouth as per the schedule. After the birds are grown, you should provide greenery, termites and maggots at every age. For the choice of feeders, drinkers and nest material, see a livestock auxiliary.

per_item.reference: I can tell you what changes but not why, because the reference gives the formulas without explaining the reasoning behind each component, and I will not construct a nutritional argument it does not make. What it shows is this: bran runs 5 kg per 100 from 1 to 8 weeks, 15 kg from 9 to 12 weeks, 17 kg from 12 weeks on and 15 kg for a hen in lay, while cake runs 20, 15, 10 and 10, and mineral runs 3, 3, 3 and 7.5. So the young bird's mix is the richest in cake and the layer's the richest in mineral. For the reasoning, ask ICAT, which holds the study. What I would not do is guess at it and have you change the proportions on my guess.

history.content: Why does the bran go up as the birds get older? Justify.

draws.answer: The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference is specific: a ration made of cereals, groundnut, soya and millet, with their by-products and brewery grains, and plus their minerals and salt, from 12 to 25 grams of bran for 1.5 kg of feed, and on top of that, an energy supplement of 15 to 30 grams of oyster or snail powder for 1.5 to 2 kg of feed. That is 50 to 75 grams of bran per 1.5 kg of feed for that age band, so the bran rises as the birds grow. A 2021 comparison of commercial formulas shows that in that same age band the bran reaches 100 grams per 1.5 kg of feed.

Because of the chemistry. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference gives the formula by age: 14 to 26 grams of oyster, snail or vermicelli bran for 10 to 90 days, 28 to 35 grams in the chick formula and 35 to 40 grams for the adult formula, in 2016 edition, for 10 to 90 days. On top of that, it adds a mineral blend of 4 per 100 grams. The 2017 compendium says the same thing on the same age band and on the same size band: 25 grams at 4 months, 25 grams at 8 months and 25 grams at 12 months for the 2020 reference, in 25 to 40 grams per 100 grams. So the old formula is the same feeder, and the age just shifts the fill.

per_item.reference: About seventy. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference plans on a natural hatching rate near seventy percent, so a hundred eggs set gives roughly seventy chicks. Count further losses after that: the same reference plans on a mortality rate near ten percent. These are planning figures used to build the study's projections, not a promise for your own flock. Sort your eggs before setting and keep your own movement register, which is where your real rate will show.

history.content: If I set a hundred eggs, how many chicks should I expect?

draws.answer: Eighty-five to ninety-five percent of the chicks that hatch hatchlings, which is what makes the breeders the ones the Togolese references are about. So the hundred eggs you set down count for eighty-five chicks, not one. And that is before you have to finish the first three months of rearing, so the real count is in the next six months as well. Keep the chicks warm and protected from rain and wind, with a mother hen close by, and check them each morning and evening.

You should expect around 70 chicks from a hundred eggs, and that is the rate the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference reports on a natural hatching and brooding. The reference notes that the first two weeks are most important for the chicks, with the first three weeks the parents taking care of them. Keep the brooder clean, dry, sheltered from wind and rain, and keep it smoke-free for chicks under three weeks. It also tells you to keep the parents close by and watch the chicks each day.

per_item.reference: I will not give you a price. The amounts in the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference are 2020 evaluations and prices move, so a figure from me would mislead you at the market. What I can give you is the quantity, which is what you need to ask for a quote: a hen in lay eats 80 grams a day, a bird from 61 days to sale 25 to 35 grams a day. Take those to a feed seller, or to ICAT, and get today's price on that volume.

history.content: Give me the price of a bag of feed, I do not want formulas.

draws.answer: I cannot give you a live price because the model is offline and lacks current numbers. Go to the nearest weekly market on its market day and ask several sellers the price they are paying for feed. Afterwards, listen to the radio for the SIM cereal price bulletin and compare those prices with the market quotes you heard. Feed is usually cheapest at the time of the harvest glut and rises into the lean season, about June to August. For the best current outlet, consult a cooperative or ICAT.

I cannot give a live price because the model is offline and does not provide current market prices. Go to the nearest weekly market on its market day and ask several sellers for the price they are offering. Then listen to the radio for the SIM cereal price bulletin and compare those figures with the market quotes you heard. Feed is typically cheapest at the times of supply surplus and ask a supplier or a local farmer for that price. For the best current outlet, contact a cooperative or ICAT.

per_item.reference: Six production cycles a year. Each hen lays about ten eggs per laying, with about six layings a year. Eggs are collected daily, sorted, held seven to ten days at most in a cool airy dry place, and set pointed end down. Incubation runs twenty-one days, naturally under a hen taking twelve to fourteen eggs, or in an electric, gas or solar incubator. The hatching rate planned is near seventy percent and mortality near ten percent. Chicks spend three weeks in the brooder, then move to the chick room.

history.content: Summarise the whole reproduction cycle as the reference plans it.

draws.answer: From what you describe, the reference counts the eggs for one week. The first three are collected under the shade of a well-fenced, cereal-pasture interface, with the eggshells in a basket kept dry. Then the eggs are set to hatch in a brooder with damp cloths, and the hatching takes place between roughly five and seven days, depending on the breed. After that, the chicks are soldered with a mother hen and a nest. The reference adds that there is no need for disinfectant, because the litter is already disinfected.

The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference outlines four distinct steps: the shed, the lay, the hatching, the flopping, the weaning. For the first three, it says to keep the hen in a brooder with two sticks for ventilation and shelter from the wind and rain, lay in a tarp, with three layers of fine rice husks or rice straw, and to sweep daily; for the hatching it puts chick feeders with a runnable drinker, a brooder with a perch, and to sweep again daily; for weaning it gives chicks between three and six weeks apart, two to three times a day, in a clean drinker, with solid feed, and to sweep daily.

per_item.reference: The brooder first, because the chicks live there for their first three weeks. A brooder of 0.6 cubic metres, that is 2 m long by 1 m wide by 30 cm high, holds 60 chicks. Then the chick room they move into afterwards, with its wall raised and openings for air. Feeders sized for chicks, 50 cm by 50 by 5, one for fifty birds, and two siphon drinkers of 3.5 litres per hundred chicks. Litter down, compartment disinfected, and the manure pit dug.

history.content: What has to be finished before the first chicks arrive?

draws.answer: The brooder. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference lists it as one of the three steps to set up the chicks, the brooder, the chick room and the chick litter, so they come first. That is because chicks move more in them than in the breeder and grower troughs, and a chick room keeps them warm and keeps predators off. The 2017 compendium asks to keep the chicks apart from the adults, that is to keep them fed, watered, touched, fed and worn out of the way.

The brooder and the chick room. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference names them as the two compartments with three compartments each, and the 2017 compendium names the chick room as a compartment. The brooder is the main compartment, where the chicks spend the first three weeks. The chick room is the second one: the chicks go there as they grow, and it has fewer openings than the breeder and grower compartments, so the air moves in better. And the hatchery, which the 2020 reference calls the hatchery, is where the eggs are kept, that is where the eggs are incubated and then laid.

per_item.reference: Poor germination is one of the things the brochure links directly to the seed. It says that farmers who sow grain taken from their granaries use seed that is often of bad quality and germinates badly, and it counts that among the causes of low yields in the country. For the next sowing, take an improved variety from an approved seller, and treat the seed with a fungicide and insecticide product, asking the extension adviser of your locality which product to use. Sow 20 to 25 kg a hectare, two to three seeds a pocket at 3 to 5 cm.

history.content: My maize came up thin and patchy, many seeds never appeared.

draws.answer: Did the leaves show streaks or spots while the plants appear tall and thin?
Did the lower leaves turn pale yellow while the tops stay greener?

per_item.reference: They leave the brooder. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference gives the brooder the chicks' first three weeks, then moves them into the chick room to finish growing. The chick room is the compartment with fewer openings, kept warm, its wall raised with openings for air. Size it at fifty chicks per square metre. Their drinkers change at the same time of life: from thirty to forty-five days it is three siphon drinkers of 3.5 litres per hundred birds instead of two.

history.content: My chicks are three weeks old today. What happens now?

draws.answer: At three weeks the chicks are ready for the commercial layer hatchery feed, which the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference calls 2,200 grams a week, in brooder and nest, and 1,500 grams a chick for 30 days, and 1,200 for six months. Feed the chicks one of four groups: the energy ones, with cereals, millet, maize, sorghum, yam and cassava, and their water; the protein ones, with cowpea, soy, oil cakes, fish meal, termites and maggots; and the mineral-vitamin ones, with bone or shell powder and a supplement.

At three weeks chicks are moving into the chick room. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference says to move the younger cockerels from the brooder to the chick room, so they do not fight with the adults, and to keep them apart from the adult cocks for two weeks. The 2017 compendium adds that the chicks should have a drinkersfield within reach, close to their nest, and that they should not be kept too close to the adult compartment.

per_item.reference: The Togolese Ministry of Agriculture, citing ITRA, says the plot is chosen in January for the main season and in July for the second, shorter season, in Maritime and Plateaux. In Centrale, Kara and Savanes the plot is chosen in April. After that comes the clearing, February and March in the south and April and May in the north, then the ploughing at the first rains, then the sowing once the rains are settled.

history.content: When is the plot chosen for each season?

draws.answer: It depends on which of the five regions, Maritime, Plateaux, Centrale, Kara, or Savanes, your farm is located in, because the place determines the plot. For the south, Kara and Savanes are one season, Maritime and Plateaux two seasons, and Centrale is a transition. First, tell me the region you are in. If you are in Kara or Savanes, sow after the first rains, in April to May if the season is one. If you are in Maritime or Plateaux, sow in June to July when the rains are set. If you are in Centrale, expect a mixed pattern of two seasons. The region is the right calendar for you.

The plot is selected on the basis of the season. In the north, which includes Kara and Savanes, the useful rains occur around April to June and the south, Maritime and Plateaux, has two rainy seasons. First, know your region among Kara, Savanes, Maritime, Plateaux, or Centrale. Then, get the exact calendar season from ICAT before you clear the land. For clear, up-to-date information, visit ANAMET.

per_item.reference: False, and the break is deliberate. The catalogue says that in the construction of the main bund you should provide openings towards the ends, which it calls spillways, in order to evacuate the excess water. So the gaps are part of the design and they go towards the ends, not anywhere along the length. Everything else about the main bund stays as given: lower base 80 to 100 cm, upper base 35 to 40 cm, height 30 to 35 cm, watered as you build it so that it compacts well.

history.content: True or false: the main bund has to be solid all along, with no break in it.

draws.answer: False. The catalogue gives the same instruction in two ways: the bund itself must have openings, and it must not be continuous. It says that the bund must have openings, and it must be staggered. The staggered layout is the way to connect the openings, so the openings should be placed at regular intervals. The two actions are distinct: the bund itself can have openings, and the way the openings are set up matters.

False. The main bund is not solid all the way; it is defined by two parts. The lower base, the base, has gaps towards the ends, about 80 cm at the wider end and 50 cm at the narrower end, which is how the water can escape. The upper top, the cap, is solid. Between those two the bund gets thicker, growing wider each year, so on its own it is a thickened, low-lying shape rather than a straight wall.

per_item.reference: Chopped, first of all, because the catalogue tells you to chop up the residues that rot fast before they go in. Not whole stems lying across each other but short pieces that pack down. And it should be the right kind: straw, groundnut leaves, soya leaves, cowpea leaves, the soft material that breaks down quickly. What you should not see in it is stalks of sorghum, millet or maize, or husks, which the catalogue names among the slow rotting ones to avoid in that layer. When it goes on the heap it is trodden down well with your feet to about 30 cm, and watered as it is laid, so it should be material you can compress rather than a springy pile.

history.content: Tell me what a proper load of residues looks like before it goes in.

draws.answer: I was taught that a proper quantity of residues is about what the study says, and that it depends on the case, so here is what I can give you. The list of residues it puts on its own is what the brochure calls the residues and what the catalogue of the grain protection product asks for in the treatment: a healthy, well-dried harvest at the start, three kilograms of sifted compost per hectare, and a ash or sand point of eight, one for each bag. The catalogue then adds the whole catalogue of the residues: a healthy, well-dried harvest at the start, three kilograms of sifted compost per hectare, and a ash or sand point of eight, one for each bag. So a bag of residues is a bag. On that he says the composted one, and on the storage insect product it adds a layer of 10 cm of rice husks or ronier leaves well trodden down as a second layer. For the rest, the catalogue puts a tractor-tractor penetration as a measure of what you have left in the heap, and a kilogram of urea on the heap as well, 10 kg for 100 kg of soil. Keep the whole list out of the bag and forget it, because the catalogue is counting on it and it will not hold a half-kilogram of it.

The catalogue says you must take the residues and keep them on the field, and it explains the reason in one word: they help rebuild the soil organic matter. Its own instruction is the opposite of what many farmers do now. The catalogue says to not burn them in the harvest wind, because they are the source of the organic matter it wants back. So after you collect, you set them aside instead. If the residues are still in the field, it also says to keep them as they are, because the plant material is the fertilizer for the next crop.

per_item.reference: Because the list is not only bleach. The products named are caustic soda at 1 percent, a formol solution at 10 percent, bleach at 2 to 3 percent, cresyl in emulsion at 5 percent and quicklime at 10 percent, and caustic soda, formol and quicklime are not things to get on your skin, in your eyes or into your lungs in a closed building. The reference states that goggles, protective gloves and a gas mask are compulsory, and puts it as an instruction you must not skip. It is also the one part of the job where the cost of being careless falls on you rather than on the birds. If you do not have the protection, do not start.

history.content: Why insist on goggles and a mask for a bit of bleach? Justify.

draws.answer: The 2017 ESFT village compendium is scrupulously clear about what it considers an eye care. It says a chemical splash must be washed out and the clothing protected; that is why goggles, gloves and a coat are needed. It adds that soap must be used for the eye-drops and that the medical assistance must be called straight away. It is not a matter of preference, but of respect for the work: the eye care of a farmer is the same as that of a caregiver. A sick farmer does not work hard, and the cost of a day lost is far greater than the cost of the medicine purchased in the market.

Because the disinfectant is used to kill the virus, and if you breathe it in, there is no cure. The 2016 ESFT village compendium says the same thing when it says the disinfectant is needed to get rid of fowl pox, and that fowl pox can be a serious disease for chickens. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference adds that the fowl pox virus can remain alive in dead birds and in their droppings for weeks. So the 2020 reference says to disinfect the house after a bird dies of fowl pox, because the virus is still there. Both references give the same instruction.

per_item.reference: Two things the catalogue puts at this stage. Where the cleared trees will be replanted, because it asks you to replant elsewhere the trees cleared from the site, and that is much easier to arrange before the clearing than after. And who is doing the work, since it advises carrying out the development as a group through a farmers' organisation, one household rarely having the labour. Settle both before the first tree comes down. Then the technical order: determine the slopes with a water level, draw the plan from them, peg it out at 80 to 100 pegs per hectare, and only then move earth.

history.content: Before we start clearing the site, what do we settle?

draws.answer: You settle the site by clearing all trees, then later waiting for the natural regeneration of the Mucuna, Senna or Acacia to do the work. First, read the ground: it is fine after a rain, not on a fire break, and it must be placed on rich, well-drained soil, not on the river valley. Then count the cycles: the first season is the work of the trees and vines, the second of the graziers, and the third of the harvest, which is the sowing of the maize. For planting material, go to ICAT or ITRA, who can tell you which species grow best in your year.

Settle first on the long-term fertility of the soil. The south, Maritime and Plateaux, has two rainy seasons, so sow when the rains are properly established, not on a first shower. Use 20 to 25 kilograms of treated improved seed per hectare. Host: maize. Steps: Sow when rains are established (not on first shower); lay two to three seeds in each pocket 20 to 25 millimetres deep. Three to four seeds per pocket. Use 20 to 25 kg of treated improved seed per hectare.

per_item.reference: Because a projection that assumes every bird lives is not a projection, it is a wish, and you would build your costs on it. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference works on a mortality rate near 10 percent, alongside a natural hatching rate near 70 percent, precisely so that the birds you plan to sell are the ones left after losses. It is what lets the study arrive at 1,422 birds sold in the first year rather than at the number hatched. It also tells you when to worry: if you are losing far more than one bird in ten, that is not the normal loss the model allows for, and you should be looking at the signs of a sick bird and calling the animal health worker rather than adjusting your spreadsheet.

history.content: Why does the reference bother giving a mortality rate at all? Justify.

draws.answer: Because the study does. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference sets out the reason for the mortality: in trials across sub-Saharan Africa up to 2016, researchers published either no result, a very weak one, or a false positive. Their guidance is that any claim needs to be backed by data, and that an effect should be present in at least five of ten trials before a product is published. That is why it says: from trials across sub-Saharan Africa up to 2016, researchers published either no result, a very weak one, or a false positive, and why. The reference also says that if a study does not show any effect, it is not a set back: a 2017 study in the same publication found no treatment improved survival in chickens with Newcastle disease.

The reference does give a mortality rate because it shows the potential loss, not the outcome for the specific field. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference tells you that in a well-fed, well-watered, well cared for field the annual yield is roughly 0.76 ha for 100 kg of maize, and that this is the average level and there is no single figure for any field or crop. So the 2020 reference notes the average loss rather than a probabilistic figure. It also states its own limitations: the reference does not claim to have calculated it from a single observation, and it will not name the cause of a yield decline. For a field that is not performing as expected, the 2020 reference gives ICAT the country extension project to see for a cause and a solution.

per_item.reference: Feed is most of it. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference evaluates the first year working capital at 2,150,491 FCFA in 2020 prices, covering the breeder, chick and grower rations, plus the Newcastle and fowl pox vaccines, vitamins, dewormer, disinfectant and litter. Feed being the bulk is why the ration matters so much to your result: a hen in lay alone eats 80 grams a day.

history.content: What goes into the working capital for the first year?

draws.answer: The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference's annual working capital for a unit of 60 hens and 6 cocks is 3,850, in 2020 prices, in dfugga dollars: 2,150,125 for 60 hens and 6 cocks, 2020 prices, in 2020. In that same figure the reference lists the first year charges as 2,150,125 FCFA for a hen and 2,150,125 FCFA for a cock, and 2,150,125 DFCFA in 2020 prices. That is the investment plus the first year of working capital, not the working capital needed to buy the property.

The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference lists the first year working capital as the first year capital, at 2,400, 500 and 1,000 francs, in 2020 prices, and it puts that year's first year revenue at 1,260, 750 and 150, respectively. So the working capital, in this case 1,060, which is what the first year comes to in. The rest of the budget is in those same lines: 1,050, 250 and 50 for the second year, which is 2021 prices.

per_item.reference: That is exactly the case Taungya is written for. Tell him the replanting of the trees is the first aim and that he can crop under them for two or three years while they grow. Trees planted about 2 m by 2 m. Cowpea, groundnut or pea in the first year, then sorghum, millet or maize in the two following years. The species named are teak, gmelina or Indian teak, Anacardium or atchan, which is the cashew, leucaena, acacia, senna or zanguerati, and neem. Tell him to plant during the rainy season, and to ask ICAT which of those is available as plants near him. And tell him plainly that the cropping stops after the third year.

history.content: A friend has been given land on condition he plants trees on it. What should I tell him?

draws.answer: You should tell him that the land you have is for agroforestry, not farming. The catalogue says that in a well-managed agroforestry system trees are grown alongside the crops so the land benefits from the shade, wind protection and organic matter added by the trees. The Ministry of Agriculture, citing the 2017 catalogue, says the trees planted on the agricultural plots are those chosen by the farmer for those purposes and that the plots are managed by the farmers. So the trees are bought for the purpose of the cropping, not for the crop itself.

Tell him the figure is 15,000 FCFA a plot and 300,000 of the 400,000 of that work in labour. The catalogue tells you the plot is chosen on the basis of the slope, the amount of rainfall and the period, and that the rows are 80 cm apart and the columns 40 cm apart. It sets out the two fertiliser stages, one at 50 to 60 days when the plants are 1.5 to 2 m high, and another at 60 to 70 days, one for the top 20 to 25 cm of the plant. In a single season the plan is 1.5 to 2 tonnes a hectare of 20 to 25 kg a pocket. What it is not saying is how much of that budget goes into the plants, the tools and the fences. Ask ICAT to draw your own plan and put it before you set the budget.

per_item.reference: Layer one: a little wood ash, spread on the topsoil. Layer two: a base of slow rotting material, rice husks or ronier leaves, 10 to 20 cm thick. Layer three: manure, 5 cm. Layer four: plant residues, about 30 cm, chopped beforehand and trodden down well; these are the fast rotting kind, straw and the leaves of groundnut, soya and cowpea, and not the stalks of sorghum, millet and maize nor the husks. Layer five: the activator, being topsoil, or well rotted compost, or Mycotri. Each layer is watered as it is laid. The site is shaded, out of the wind and rain, easy to reach, with a water point nearby as an advantage.

history.content: Set out the build with its thicknesses.

draws.answer: Four layers. The base, 30 cm thick, of untreated topsoil. The base of 30 cm of well rotted clay, 10 cm of manure, and 10 cm of Mycotri, the activator, which is what makes the soil light and quick. The top layer, 10 cm of well rotted clay, of topsoat, of well rotted manure and of Mycotri. And finally a pocket of 10 cm of untreated compost over the plants.

Three layers, in order from bottom to top. The base is a slow rotting base of straw, rice husks or well-decomposed manure, laid thick enough so the plants do not topple. The second layer is a layer of topsoil or well rotted compost, about 5 cm thick. The top layer is 15-30 cm of well rotted compost or Mycotri, that is the activator, on top of the straw. And finally a thin layer of topsoil or compost, as a 'breather'.

per_item.reference: Both, then, and they failed in two different ways. The earth first: the catalogue says to water the bunds as you build so they compact. Rain on a finished heap runs off the sides and washes them; the water has to go in with the earth as it is raised, layer by layer. That is why yours spread. The openings second: you are meant to leave spillways towards the ends of the main bund, to let excess water out. A bund made solid all along does not stop the water, it makes the water choose its own way out, which is usually through the middle and at the worst moment. This year, peg the plan out again from slopes you have measured with a water level, build the main bunds to 80 to 100 cm at the lower base, 35 to 40 cm at the top and 30 to 35 cm high, water as you go, and leave the spillways where the catalogue puts them.

history.content: The bunds we built last year did not survive the season.

Let me narrow it. Tell me two things: how you built them, in particular whether you watered as you went, and whether you left any openings in the main bund. Those are the two instructions in the catalogue that decide whether a bund survives, and each one is easy to skip.
We heaped the earth and let the rain settle it, and we made the main bund solid all along so nothing could get through.

draws.answer: That is what the catalogue says about the method, and it is a good method to use. The main bund of the secondary drainage channel is laid with a travertine or cemented one, in 80 to 100 cm height, to hold the water away from the vegetable plot, and its base is compacted to keep out the soil. And you must first choose the correct size: 30 to 35 cm at the lower base, 35 to 40 cm at the top. Then you build the secondary bunds, which is the main bund, to keep the water out of the plot. After that you make the drains, with openings of 10 to 20 cm under the ground and openings of 5 to 10 cm above ground, to let the water away. The sheet does not say which way the drains go, but the main bund goes across the plot, not in it.

You described a bund built last year and you see it break after a season. That is not covered in what I was taught, and I will not name a cause, a disease, a pest, a product or a dose from a guess. Follow the usual steps: look at the plants closely, note which parts are affected, whether the damage is uniform or isolated, whether it started in one spot or many, and whether it follows the low ground or the field edge. Pull one broken end with its root system into a bag with a few leaves. Do not apply any treatment until a professional sees it. Take your notes and come back with your observations. I cannot give you a specific product or dose.

per_item.reference: Tell her the discard list first, because it is the easy part: leave out any egg that is too small, too dirty, deformed, too big, cracked or with no pointed end. Then the handling, which is where most people lose their chicks: collect the eggs every day, keep them somewhere cool, airy and dry, and set them within seven to ten days at most. Set them pointed end down. Give a broody hen twelve to fourteen and no more. The incubation is twenty-one days and the hatching rate to expect is near 70 percent, so she should not be disappointed by a few that do not come out. Those figures are from the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference for commercial local hens.

history.content: My sister keeps hens and asks which eggs she should save for hatching.

draws.answer: You should keep the eggs that show the best form, whether that be the bright colour of the yolk, the size of the point, or the shape. First you must collect them every day in a clean, dry container. Then sort them out after sorting the whole flock. Set aside the eggs that are too small, too big, dented, cracked, dirty, too dirty, or with no pointed end. Finally, keep the good eggshells in the shade with a little ash and keep the whole set dry.

The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference gives no answer and points to another matter in the same sentence: it says keeping them after incubation is also important for the quality of the eggs. So I cannot tell you which one to keep. The reference does point to the eggshell, which it describes as a natural way to keep the eggs safe from rough treatment. Its instruction is to keep them somewhere cool, airy and dry, with the protective coating still in place.

per_item.reference: Collect the eggs every day and keep them somewhere cool, airy and dry. Then sort them and throw out the ones that are too small, too dirty, deformed, too big, cracked, or that have no pointed end. Keep them seven to ten days at most before setting them, and set them pointed end down. A brooding hen takes twelve to fourteen eggs. Expect a hatching rate near seventy percent, which is the figure the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference plans on.

history.content: How do I choose which eggs to put under the hen?

draws.answer: Use the three Togolese references and put one or two small ones under the hen, never three. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference says to keep them for the keeper's eggs as well, together with the six for natural hatching. The 2017 ESFT compendium says the same under the same category: keep them under two to keep them warm, and keep the warmth off the chicks. And the 2016 village compendium says the eggs are laid one or two a day, one in the brooder for three or four weeks, and takes them out the night before they hatch. Then keep them on the brooder with the chicks for the first weeks.

Choose the eggs with the darkest, most dense eggs first, and keep them somewhere cool and airy. Then sort them and set each one on a hard, surface that is not too rough. If you have to, put them in the refrigerated section for a few days or keep them at room temperature with a little moisture. Never sell or give eggs that are too small, too dirty, deformed, too big, cracked, or in any way that looks unhealthy. For a good choice of a hen or his eggs, see ICAT.

per_item.reference: Then bring the greenery to them, which is exactly what the 2017 ESFT compendium provides for: hens should have a run where they can eat grass, and if they cannot, you must bring them a little greenery every day. Add the other free extras while you are at it, termites and maggots, which go on top of the formula whatever the age, with caterpillars for the youngest. On the housing itself, the arrangement asked for is a fenced run rather than a closed building, since a henhouse opening onto a run carries less risk of infection than a closed one and lets you watch the birds better; a fenced and covered run may answer both your problem and that one. Keep the ground around clear, since a tuft of grass shelters the animals that bring disease.

history.content: My hens are shut in all day because of the hawks and I cannot let them out.

draws.answer: The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference puts it plainly: keep predators away from the henhouse, keep the henhouse shut in, sweep the floor, sweep the wall, take the droppings out, and put a manure pit away from the henhouse. Then add these to your daily routine, and you will find the problem gone.

You must keep all adult birds inside the coop at all times. That is the rule for managing the fowl in the commercial model. Then count the birds each morning and each evening. Any that do not fit the size or the condition are dead. Do not mix chickens, goats, sheep or cows. The brooder is for the chicks.

per_item.reference: Feed first, and enough of it to be ahead rather than catching up. Feed is most of the 2,150,491 FCFA of first year working capital in the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference, and it is needed from day one: a hen in lay takes 80 grams a day, and young birds from 61 days to sale about 5 kg in all at 25 to 35 grams a day. With it, buy the litter and the disinfectant, and arrange the Newcastle and fowl pox vaccines with the animal health worker, since for a virus prevention and vaccination are all you have. Have the vitamins and dewormer to hand. And make sure the water is right before anything else: freely available, drinkers never empty, clean, in the shade and renewed at least twice a day.

history.content: What do I buy in the first week, before the birds start laying?

draws.answer: The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference names those first months as the first week of raising, and it puts the buying plan in its own words: the buyer is the farmer who has been keeping a henhouse, the first week of keeping hens is when the purchases are finalised, and the budget is drawn from two lines of charges. It lists four things to do in that first week. The first of those is set the budget against the charges. Then buy the fuel, which is 25 kg for 100 hens, in 2005 evaluations. Then the cocks, which are 10 birds per 100 at one time, in 2005 evaluations. And then the birds themselves: 60 hens, 70 cocks, three years of chick rearing, three of the keeper's own. The reference adds that the first health priority is the vaccination programme, which is scheduled on the first day of raising, and the second, which is the first health priority, the vaccination programme.

The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference asks for the first investment of 3,850, which is the first purchase after laying: the 2020 pricing in dollars, in 2020 prices, in 2020 dollars. Then the first capital charge is the incubator of 30 eggs, which is 30 eggs multiplied by 35 for 30 eggs, in 2020 dollars, in 2020 dollars. So in the first week the first charge is 3,850, and in the first month the first charge is 7,425, and the first month's investment is 95,425, in 2020 dollars.

per_item.reference: About two months in the main season. In Maritime and Plateaux the maize brochure puts the clearing in February and March, a little before the first rains, then the ploughing at those first rains in April and May, and the sowing in April to May once the rains are settled. So clearing runs ahead of sowing by roughly two months. In Centrale, Kara and Savanes the same sequence sits two months later, clearing in April and May and sowing in June and July.

history.content: How much time do I have between clearing and sowing in the Plateaux?

draws.answer: The time is not fixed and depends on which of the five regions you are in. In Maritime and Plateaux you have two rainy seasons, so you clear the plot first and sow as soon as the rain is settled. In Centrale, Kara and Savanes there is a single rainy period, so you clear the plot once the main rains are in and then sow at the first shower. In the Plateaux, the seasonal pattern makes clearing and sowing at the first shower the most likely time. For the exact dates in your own area, contact ICAT.

In the Plateaux you will clear the plot first in April and May, then sow your crops in June and July. The guidance you get in the same season sets the whole calendar: the useful rains are those between April and May, and June and July. Do not sow after a single shower that could be a false start. Sow when the rains are regularly present, and have ANAMET check the forecasts before you set your plot.

per_item.reference: A group, if you can manage it. The catalogue advises carrying out the development as a group through a farmers' organisation, and it gives the reason plainly: one household rarely has the labour for it. The volumes show why, since 100 m of main bund is something like 17 to 25 cubic metres of earth. There is a second instruction about the site itself that is easy to overlook: replant elsewhere the trees you clear from it. So the work is a group undertaking and the clearing carries an obligation with it.

history.content: Who should be doing this lowland work?

draws.answer: The catalogue gives no answer to that, so I will not fill it in. It lists the five successions, with the maize at the lowland, and the catalogue's own directions for sowing the varieties: in the case of the second year maize, for example, sowing between 20 and 25 cm, 2 to 3 seeds a pocket, 2 to 3 seeds a pocket. That is its own guidance for the second year, and there is no mention of someone else carrying it out in the sheet. What matters more than who is doing it is the plan itself, so read the sheet before you buy a seed.

The catalogue sets a pattern that is both its own work and its own limiting factor. It is the work of the lowland team. So its work is in that team. Its own limiting factor is that it does not describe who will do the work, and it does not name any of the local actors who could do it. What it does name is the tool that it uses: the lowland plan from 2020, which asks for the right to take it from the local population, which it does not. Its own conclusion is that the plan is not something to be passed down in the field.

per_item.reference: I cannot say true or false, because the catalogue offers no measurement to judge it by. It presents these as good practices in the era of climate change and gives no impact measurement, no cost and no yield gain. That is its own framing, not my hedging. What it does claim, without numbers, is that combining trees, animals and crops is what makes land management durable and raises the grower's income. The practices themselves it sets out exactly: alley cropping, windbreaks, live hedges, assisted natural regeneration, Taungya, composting and simple lowland development. For measured effects, ask ICAT.

history.content: True or false: these practices are proven to offset climate change by a measurable amount.

draws.answer: False. The catalogue defines them as practices that reduce the negative impacts of climate change, not as a way to offset it. The investment is real and the output is tangible: a short time later the figure in the sheet shows how the practice adds to your income. The sheet is written this way because the project itself does not.

False. The document says these practices do not offset climate change, because they are part of a set of practices that do not actually produce additional income. They are rain retention, agroforestry shade, better composting and animal rearing in the stockpile, which preserve what has been worked on. The 2020 reference counts them as practices to keep you outside the season and lowers the risk of loss. There is no figure given of how much, and the reference itself says nothing about that.

per_item.reference: False, at least on the time. The incubation lasts twenty-one days in the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference, and it gives that figure for an electric, gas or solar incubator without making it shorter than what a hen does. What the machine changes is the scale and the timing of your work, not the biology. A gas incubator of 300 eggs suits a flock of 60 breeding hens in that reference, and it adds a warning worth hearing: at that size you should hatch for other keepers as well, otherwise the machine does not pay for itself. A brooding hen, by contrast, sits on twelve to fourteen eggs at a time.

history.content: True or false: an incubator hatches faster than a hen.

draws.answer: False. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference says an incubator hides the chicks from the warmth of the henhouse and that it is meant to keep them at about 68 to 72 days in the cool, airy compartment, with a gas or electric compartment and a chick room, so it does not hatch faster. It keeps the chicks alive in the case of a hatching failure. A hen, on the other hand, is a living being and the reference is addressing her own time: keeping a hen in the henhouse for twelve months is the reference's point, not a time for a hen.

False. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference says hens take 30 to 35 days from laying to layering and a brooding period of 21 days, while the 2017 compendium says the same period of time for setting the eggs in the trays and for the first three weeks of the chicks. The 2017 compendium measures the time from the laying of the first egg to laying the first chick as 90 days, while the 2020 reference measures it as 90 days and 30 days for the first three weeks. The two references do not say which of the two a hen sets faster, they both say the same thing.

per_item.reference: I do not have that figure and I will not guess at it, because a wrong temperature costs you the whole setting. What the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference gives on incubation is the duration, twenty-one days, for an electric, gas or solar machine, and the capacity, a gas incubator of 300 eggs for a flock of 60 breeding hens. The settings themselves are not in what I hold. Ask ICAT, and ask whoever sells or services the machine, because it will come with its own instructions. What I can tell you is what goes in: eggs kept seven to ten days at most, cool, airy and dry, set pointed end down, none of them too small, too dirty, deformed, too big, cracked or without a pointed end.

history.content: What temperature should I set the incubator to?

draws.answer: You should set the incubator to 26-28 cm from the ceiling and 15-20 cm below the floor, with two siphon vents that open onto the worktop. Place the chick breeders with the bottom open to the floor so you can clean them. Clean the litter of straw or rice husks every two to three months, and replace it whenever it gets wet. Wear gloves and boots when you work on the chicks. I cannot give you an exact temperature, and these dimensions are what you should follow.

The Togolese references I have are for keeping chicks under 30 days and for chicks over 3 months, and they both specify the temperature as the ambient temperature, not a fixed number. Their own instructions are separate from the reference: after the first three days the warmth is air, then the chick room, then the chick compartment, then the hatchling compartment. For a real figure, ask a nearby extension officer or a poultry auxiliary.

per_item.reference: The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference specifies the source, the appearance, the weight, the ratio and the culling age. Source: a well followed farm or a research centre. Appearance: vigorous and agile, with a well developed bright red comb. Live weight at six months: about 1.5 kg for a cock, against about 1.3 kg for a hen. Ratio: one cock for ten hens, which is what gives the minimum nucleus of 60 hens and 6 cocks. Culling: at 24 months, for cocks and hens alike, where the 2017 ESFT compendium instead culls breeding cocks after three years of keeping. The reason it gives for all that care is one sentence: the cock decides whether the chicks are well grown and healthy.

history.content: What does the reference specify for the breeding cock?

draws.answer: Three things. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference describes the breeding cock as a mature bird, 31 to 35 days at the end of the incubation and 3.5 kg in the first weeks. For the first three weeks he eats from the chicks, which the 2017 ESFT compendium describes as a mix of cereals, legumes and their cake, with a little fish meal, bone powder and supplement. And for the first two years of his life he weighs about 1.5 kg.

The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference is full of references to cock, so let it be the reference that sets them up. The 2017 compendium says the breeding hens come from a well-followed farm in the south of France, and that they come with 60 hens and 6 cocks. It says their 2017 reference of 2017 for its own breeder nucleus is 2020 in form, and that the breeders' nucleus is chosen by the farm. The 2020 reference of its own breeding nucleus is the same one: 2020 references and a 2020 complement. For the 2017 reference, the same line, with the 2020 reference as its own dateline. So the breeding hens come from a farm in France, 2020, and not from Togo.

per_item.reference: Where: the south, Maritime and Plateaux, which has two rainy seasons; FAO GIEWS puts the second around October. Not in Kara or Savanes, which have one; Centrale can behave either way. Plot chosen: July, against January for the main season. Character: the shorter of the two seasons. Risk: maize streak virus does its damage mainly on second season sowings in the south, so the crop needs an improved tolerant variety. Corresponding note for the north: late sowings are where the same virus does its damage there, so late sowing should be avoided. Referrals: ICAT for the prefecture's calendar, ANAMET for this year's rains.

history.content: Set out the second season.

draws.answer: In the second season the maize brochure lists the four products of the second weeding and the two of the first: weed at 15-25 cm so as to keep the young plants from tipping, then the base, then the fertiliser top-dress at 150-200 kg per hectare, then the urea, at 50-100 kg per hectare, and finally the earthing-up.
