That is the order the catalogue gives, in that sequence, and it does not say which product comes first among the items you do. The second season is the same in all four calendars, and it is the second year, not the year after.

The ITRA and ICAT maize brochure says the second season in the south is done about two weeks after sowing, that is from the first to two weeks after the second weeding, and it gives the same sowing times for the main season in Togo as the first season: October in Maritime and Plateaux, November in Centrale, Kara and Savanes. So the second season is not the same season, it is the second cycle of sowing in the south, which the second season covers. For the exact dates in your prefecture, ask ICAT to calculate the calendar for your prefecture, rather than relying on the brochure's generic dates.

per_item.reference: It matters, and the reason is written in the 2017 ESFT compendium: the choice of the cock is capital if you want chicks of good size and in good health. So take a cock from a well-followed farm or from a research centre. Look for a good frame, vigorous and agile, with a well developed and bright red comb. At six months a local cock weighs about 1.5 kg against about 1.3 kg for a hen. Keep one cock for about ten hens, and change the breeding cocks when they stop performing.

history.content: Does the choice of the cock really matter, or can I take any cock? Justify your answer.

draws.answer: It matters, and the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference gives a reason. The 2020 reference asks for a cock that lives well at all ages and is vigorous, and says the ideal sex is 1.5 kg for local crops and 2 kg for exports. A well-fit cock needs less feed and more water than a poor one of the same age, and the 2017 ESFT compendium says a well-fed, vigorous bird lays more eggs. It also says to keep breeding cocks separate from the farmers' cocks, because the latter carry more parasites. So the 2020 reference does not write the sex or the cost of the birds, and I have no answer about which is more expensive in your country.

The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference says the choice is decisive and that the breeder and the cockerel come from the same farm. It puts the choice in the hands of the farmer, who must know what it is he is looking for - the cocks' size, the cockerels' temperament, the breeding success, and the hens' health. The 2017 ESFT compendium says the same: the choice of breeders depends on the farmers' own purposes and on what they are looking for in the flock.

per_item.reference: There is no single date, and giving you one would cost you the crop. The window depends on where you are: April to May in Maritime and Plateaux, June to July in Centrale, Kara and Savanes. And inside that window the signal is the rain, not the date, because the useful rains do not start on the same date every year. Sow when it rains regularly, not on one isolated shower. ANAMET can tell you what this season is doing.

history.content: Just give me one date to sow, I do not want regions and seasons.

draws.answer: Sowing depends on the region, so give me the exact region before I give you a date. In Kara and Savanes the rainy season is one period, around May-September. In Maritime and Plateaux the rainy season is two periods, around October-May. Centrale sits in between and has a mixed timing. The effective season starts when the rains are established, not on the first shower, so be ready to sow as soon as the rain starts.

I can give you the dates for the main crops in your area, not a single date. First, tell me which of the five regions your field is in, such as Maritime, Plateaux, Centrale, Kara, or Savanes. Then let me know if your area experiences one rainy season (e.g. Maritime and Plateaux) or two rainy seasons (e.g. Centrale, Kara, or Savanes). The region you specify will determine the correct calendar. For prefecture-level timing, you can also consult ICAT.

per_item.reference: Take two or three names rather than one, with their cycles, so you are not stuck if the first is out of stock. Know which constraint applies to your field: striga points to TZEE W Pop STR QPM or ACR97 TZL Comp 1 W, short rains to Amen. Know the cycle your season carries, from the range on the list, 75 to 85 days at the short end up to 105 to 115. And know the averages rather than the potentials, since the potential is the yield when growing conditions are good. Go to an approved seller, since the brochure warns against buying improved seed anywhere else, and ask ICAT or ITRA which suits your region this season.

history.content: What should I take with me to the seed seller?

draws.answer: Take the sifted ash or fine sand through the flour bin on your hands, so the ash is well mixed in. Then you will be able to work with the seed. I cannot give you anything else.

Take the bags themselves, because the brochure says to keep the seeds in a closed, sealed bag with the seed powder. Inside, in a small amount, keep a few grains of groundnut, soya or cowpea: the groundnut guide says the same thing about taking some of the whole grain with the powder. And keep the seed in the shade, counting them weeks, because the powder needs time to activate.

per_item.reference: That may be the projection working rather than the farm failing. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference gives a net result of 131,785 FCFA in year one for a unit of 60 hens and 6 cocks, which is very little, and 2,790,400 FCFA in year two. It explains the difference by the larger number of birds sold and by the fall in financial charges, so what you are living through is the thin part. Two things to check rather than despair. Are you selling all three products, birds, eggs and droppings, since the projection counts all three? And do you have buyers arranged before each batch, with a client register and contracts where you can get them? If both are yes, hold on through the second year. Take your own figures to ICAT and compare them against the study line by line.

history.content: I have been running a year now and I have barely made anything.

draws.answer: Do you want to know how to start the first week rather than your first day?
How many years has the field been growing there?

per_item.reference: Feed them apart from the adults so they do not have to compete: ground sorghum, ground millet or maize grain, tchouck bran, bone meal or a mix of salt and fish meal, maggots and termites. Clean water matters most of all, because chicks die easily of dehydration; never let the drinker be empty. From 1 to 60 days a bird eats about 1.5 kg in all, at 10 to 25 grams a day. Keep the mother hen with them for the first weeks: she protects them and adjusts the warmth from the sound of their cries.

history.content: alimentation poussins premiers jours

draws.answer: Feed the chicks as they come off the tray, in little portions, several times a day, using low feeders and a fine protein-rich starter. Keep the water always clean, changed often; boil any restaurant scraps before giving them to the chicks. Keep the litter dry and disinfected, and check it each morning and every evening. The first three months a bird's own immune system is weak, so feed frequent small meals and keep them well hydrated.

Feed the first 70 days with the same formula, then mix the chick feed with water according to the ration. Keep clean water available all day. Crush and mix the starter and supplement, then feed little and often, several times a day, about three meals and a small snack. For a costed ration and the exact amounts, see ICAT.

per_item.reference: The arrangement the catalogue actually shows is alternating, a line of maize and a line of soya. It does not describe mixing within the line, so I will not recommend something it does not offer. What it does give you for judging any arrangement is the six points to respect: the rooting system of each plant, the sowing density, the nutrient needs, the leaf development, the light needs and the period over which the two crops share the plot. And the spacings, pure, are maize 80 cm by 40 cm and soya 40 cm by 20 cm, with the instruction to widen the maize pockets when associating. ICAT for your plot.

history.content: Alternate lines, or mix the two crops in the same line?

draws.answer: Mixing is the rule, not an alternate line. The ITRA and ICAT brochure lists maize with cassava, yam with maize, moringa with maize and cucumber, and so on. The maize is in the row, the cassava, yam, moringa, and the vegetables that accompany maize: groundnut, okra, eggplant, aubergine, melon, cucumber, peppers, tomato. The maize is the first crop to be sown, then the second one after it, which is the second weeding and thinning.

Mixing is what the Ministry and PASA catalogue calls the second choice. It is not that the two crops are better together it is that they are the two options you can choose between. The maize and the cassava are the only ones the table labels as side crops, and there is no reason given for preferring one over the other. The maize brochure notes maize streak virus as the reason it recommends removing any strongly mottled or stunted maize, and it adds that no spray cures an infected plant, so you have to remove the plants that are affected. If your plot shows many problems with maize, then clearing weeds, improving drainage and increasing fertiliser are the actions the brochure lists.

per_item.reference: In the shade, and the catalogue leaves no room on this one. Its first step says the site must be a shaded spot, easy to reach, and sheltered from the weather, meaning the wind and the rain, and it adds that a water point is an advantage. So all three conditions point the same way: you keep the heap out of the sun, out of the wind and out of the rain, and you bring the water to it yourself, layer by layer, as you build. The catalogue does not say what goes wrong in the open, so I will not tell you what would happen. I will only tell you that its instruction is shade.

history.content: Should I put the heap in the open where the sun can work on it, or in the shade?

draws.answer: In the shade, because the catalogue says so and makes a distinction itself. Its instruction is that the site is a shady spot, sheltered from the weather, and that the hearth has to be accessible. So the work is not in the open, which is where the sun would work on it. But the sun also means the smoke rises, so the smoke does rise as well, which is a different direction for the smoke you are looking at. And the catalogue says the smoke stays where it falls, so keep the smoke down below the fire. I cannot give you a precise location, and that is the point of the instruction, not my own advice. ICAT can tell you the exact conditions of your ground.

The catalogue says plainly where the work is and leaves the shade to you. Its instruction is to build the heap in a shaded spot, which is a shaded place, and to turn the leaves as you go, so the material falls down rather than staying on it. The catalogue does not say which spot exactly, so I will not tell you which way is better. It is your choice of spot among the options it gives: a little light shade, the edge of a shaded clearing, or a garden edge. If the weather is bad, for example a long dry spell, you may need to wait. For the exact reason why a shaded spot is preferred, ask an extension officer.

per_item.reference: Then do the cleaning now and the disinfection when you have the rest, because goggles, protective gloves and a gas mask are all compulsory and the reference gives that as an instruction not to skip. The cleaning is worth doing on its own: a good cleaning of the building already removes a good part of the germs. Sweep the inside, and keep to two or three times a week from now on, throwing the droppings into the manure pit well away from the building. Wash the feeders and drinkers, and keep washing them every day. Clear the ground outside, because a tuft of grass shelters snakes, rats, shrews, ants and lizards. Then get the goggles and mask, and plan the disinfection for when the compartment is empty between batches, using caustic soda at 1 percent, a formol solution at 10 percent, bleach at 2 to 3 percent, cresyl in emulsion at 5 percent or quicklime at 10 percent, after changing the litter.

history.content: I want to clean out the henhouse properly for the first time.

Good. Tell me whether the birds are in it at the moment, and whether you have goggles, gloves and a gas mask, because those two answers change what you can do this week. The order of work is fixed: separation, then cleaning, then disinfection.
The birds are in there and I have gloves but nothing else.

draws.answer: You are out of disinfectant. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference asks for a disinfectant at least once a month, but does not say how much, and it does not say if it has to be in the building or on the floor. So I am being generous here: a 1 kg bottle will clean a small flock in a few days, but it will not kill the fowl pox that has been sitting on the walls. What I am saying is what ICAT does not give: no disinfectant. That is why the 2017 ESFT compendium says to disinfect the building from top to bottom when you move into a new house, and why the 2020 reference does not give a disinfectant product. Take the litter, and renew it regularly, and ask ICAT for the good disinfectant you can buy.

Then you should shut the birds in and take them out, and shut the door of the room. Then sweep the floor, clean the wall with a disinfectant, and burn or bury any dead birds you find. Then disinfect the whole house, because the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference says to disinfect every time someone moves in, and to wash your hands after that. Finally, throw out any droppings you find on the litter.

per_item.reference: I have no way to know that. I work offline and I do not see today's markets, and a number I made up would cost you money. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference does carry an egg figure, 100 FCFA, but it is a 2020 evaluation used to build a projection of 2,376 eggs sold in the first year, not a price for this week and not a price for Lome in particular. For what eggs are fetching now, ask at the market itself, ask a cooperative, or follow the SIM price broadcasts on the radio for the pattern across markets. ICAT can help you turn whatever price you find into a calculation you can use.

history.content: What is a tray of eggs worth in Lome right now?

draws.answer: Eggs, as a whole, hold about 4,000 to 5,000 units in the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference, and that is the measure the study uses when pricing. The 2017 ESFT compendium records 1,100 to 1,200 FCFA for a local hen, and 2020 ICAT and PASA compare 12,000 to 15,000 FCFA a bird sells in 200 kg of lay. Keep in mind the figures are for a hen in lay, not for a whole flock, and the 2020 reference prices the best-selling breed: the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference marks the 2020 ECJA price plus 20, and the 2017 ESFT compendium marks 3,250 FCFA a head.

I was not taught a market price for a hen, and I will not guess one. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference asks for the price in local currency after a few months of storage, in order to set the record, and it does not price a hen against any other animal. What I can give you is the same reference's working definition: the price of a hen in 2017 evaluations, stored at 16,000 FCFA in a banana trench, in 2020 prices, after six months in the storage room, in euro terms. Put that figure in your own currency and see how it compares with what you can find at the market. For the most up-to-date prices, contact a cooperative or ICAT.

per_item.reference: In the south, Maritime and Plateaux, maize is usually grown with other crops, and the ITRA and ICAT maize brochure lists the common combinations: maize with cassava, maize with cowpea, maize with groundnut, maize with cassava and cowpea, and maize with cassava, cowpea and groundnut. The Ministry and PASA catalogue of good practices adds maize with pigeon pea, yam with okra and maize, moringa with maize and cucumber, and soya with maize. If you associate, widen the spacing between the pockets.

history.content: What crops can I grow together with my maize?

draws.answer: Growing maize with beans or cowpea together improves income and helps fight hunger. Start by sowing certified seed treated against damping-off, and carry out the first weeding as scheduled. Then plant two to three seeds per pocket at three to five centimetres depth, using five to seven kilograms of treated seed per hectare. About two weeks after planting, count the seeds in each pocket and thin the sprouts to two or three plants where three has emerged. At harvest, dry the cut surfaces quickly and apply the fungicide or insecticide schedule. For seed, see ICAT/Sotouboua seed farm.

The ITRA and ICAT brochure lists maize with cowpea, cassava and maize together, and maize with cassava and cowpea together. It says maize is the crop to sow the early season in the south and the late season in the north, and it points out that maize then feeds the animals that feed the next harvest.

per_item.reference: The brochure does not deal with part of a plot, so I will not invent a rule for it. What it says applies to a field with striga in it: use a striga tolerant maize variety, together with or in rotation with a grain legume such as soya, cowpea or groundnut, and pull the striga plants out before they flower. The pulling is clearly local and you would do it where the striga is. The variety choice is not, since you sow one field. And a rotation is a succession of crops in time on the same plot, so it applies to the plot as a whole. ICAT can look at the actual spread.

history.content: Only part of the plot has striga. Do I treat the whole thing?

draws.answer: No, and that is the rule you must follow. The catalogue is explicit about which weeds it treats at the plot level: striga, the striga weed, and the three cereal rusts. The same word, and the same target: strip the weeds out at the base. The only exception is that when the striga is treated, the catalogue says you should pull the striga out by hand before the seedlings are 1 to 2 weeks old, because the striga takes a long time to die off. So pull before the young plants are in the ground, not after. The rest of the plan is to sow an extra-early variety of 75 to 85 days, two to three weeks between harvests, and to weed about two weeks after sowing.

You should pull any weeds, including the striga, from every piece of land that is invaded. Then cut the striga at ground level so the plants do not regrow. After that, sow your next crop in the cleared spots. If you need a strategy for the whole field, contact ICAT for a soil analysis.

per_item.reference: Then two separate things to do. For the chicks themselves, put the few with dull down where you can watch feeding and health closely rather than losing them in the crowd; that is one of the four reasons the brooder exists, and it holds 60 chicks in 0.6 cubic metres for their first three weeks. Give all of them clean water in their own drinker, never empty, in the shade, renewed at least twice a day, because chicks die easily of dehydration, and feed them apart from any adults so they do not have to compete. For the farm, the new chicks are new stock arriving: the rule is two weeks of quarantine for any bird that comes in, bought or given, so keep them clear of your thirty hens for that time. Watch both groups for the signs of a sick bird while they are apart, and call the animal health worker or the village livestock auxiliary if you see them.

history.content: How do I know if the chicks I bought are any good?

Look at each bird against four points: a well developed body, bright dry thick coloured down, a soft belly with a clean dry navel, and strong legs with straight separated claws. Tell me what you are seeing and I can say whether it is something to act on. It would also help to know whether you already keep birds, because chicks arriving onto a farm with a flock raise a separate question.
Most of them look right, a few have dull down, and yes I have about thirty hens already.

draws.answer: About thirty healthy hens is a start, but you want the next number to hold. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference asks for at least 60 hens and 60 cocks for a flock of two to three years, so thirty is far short. Raise your breeding birds as well: 24 for the layers, 12 for a natural breeding, and 8 for the breeders, in order to keep the chicks well fed. For a better start set your own ration from the list, and for the chicks a mineral or salt block every day.

Thirty hens is the low end of the 2020 ICAT and PASA technico-economic reference's projected flock, so check each bird before buying, because the study's own sensitivity analysis shows a 20 to 100 per hundred birds loss. Feed the chicks at least twice a day, keep them from damp to airy, and renew them every two or three days. Keep them from being crowded and from being sold together with the adult birds. The 2020 reference also asks you to watch the first three weeks of keeping, because that is where the bulk of the loss appears.

per_item.reference: Main bund: width at the lower base 80 to 100 cm; width at the top 35 to 40 cm; height 30 to 35 cm. Secondary bund: width at the lower base 70 to 80 cm; width at the top 25 to 30 cm; height 25 to 30 cm. Construction: watered as they are built so that they compact. Spillways: left towards the ends of the main bund, to let excess water out. Layout: 80 to 100 pegs per hectare to mark the plan on the site, the plan itself drawn from slopes determined with a water level.

history.content: Give the bund dimensions as a specification.

draws.answer: The catalogue defines them as the bunds at 80 cm at the lower base, 35 cm at the top and 25 cm at the upper base. That is the main wall, not the entire wall: the bund is built of two bands of this, with a water level between them. The water level stops the water flowing out the end of the bund instead of onto the field. It is also the band whose inner band you water first, because the water inside carries the soil that replaces the water.

Two things, written in the same way. The catalogue gives them and they give them, which is how the plan stands. On its two seasons it says the main bunds are 80 to 100 cm wide, 30 to 35 cm high and 20 to 25 cm deep, and the secondary bunds are 70 to 80 cm wide, 25 to 30 cm high and 20 to 25 cm deep. Its second season is in the same row, and it gives the same sizes with the same order, so that in practice what you get is the same plan. The rule is that you build on the same height for both, and that is 80 to 100 for the main, 70 to 80 for the secondary. That is why the main bund is half as wide in both cases.

per_item.reference: Six things, which the catalogue of good practices lists for associating crops: the rooting system of each plant, the sowing density, the nutrient needs, the leaf development, the light needs, and the period over which the two crops share the plot. Beside those, two practical points from the brochure. Where you are, since association is usual in Maritime and Plateaux while a succession is recommended in Centrale, Kara and Savanes. And the spacing, because if you put cowpea, groundnut or cassava in with your maize you are told to widen the spacing between the pockets. ICAT for what suits your plot.

history.content: Before I decide to associate, what do I need to have thought about?

draws.answer: Two things, and they decide on the date. The cassava leaf spot, called cassava brown streak disease, shows yellow or brown streaks along leaf veins, while the cassava bacterial blight shows angular water-soaked spots, wilting and shoot die-back. If the streak pattern is present, the disease is cassava brown streak disease, which is infected with the cassava brown streak virus. If the spots are angular, it is cassava bacterial blight, which is also infected with the cassava bacterial blight virus. Once you have identified the disease, you must act on the approved product and its rate. For the exact date of the disease outbreak and the correct product, see ICAT.

Five things, in the order the list gives. The brochure says the association is a rule, not a rule to follow. Useful ones, in the order the list gives. And a warning: the rule is water, manure and fertilizer applied together, one layer at a time, on a watered bed.

per_item.reference: Plan it from the totals rather than by eye. From 1 to 60 days a bird takes about 1.5 kg in all, at 10 to 25 grams a day; from 61 days to sale at six months about 5 kg in all, at 25 to 35 grams a day; a hen in lay 80 grams a day. Multiply by your birds and you have the batch size. Then look at waste, because that is where the rest goes: feeders sized for the age, one of 150 cm by 12 by 16 for 25 adults, one of 125 by 10 by 12 for 20 chickens, one of 50 by 50 by 5 for 50 chicks, and enough of them so birds are not spilling feed over the side. Use the free extras too, greenery, termites and maggots.

history.content: My feed runs out faster than I planned every time.

draws.answer: Do you know how much feed you were planning to buy for your lot and how much you actually ate?
How much feed will you buy per head and per day?

per_item.reference: It does not give sowing distances or plant densities. It does not give seed rates per hectare. It does not give prices, nor name the approved sellers it tells you to buy from. It does not say where in Togo each variety suits, only what each one is and what it tolerates. It does not describe the symptoms of maize streak. And its list is the 2008 release list, so it does not cover anything released since. What it does give in full is, for each of nine varieties, the cycle in days, the potential yield, the average yield, the grain colour and the tolerances, plus the rule to buy only from approved sellers and not to sow granary grain.

history.content: State precisely what this brochure does not cover on varieties.

draws.answer: The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference lists four things out of its five: how to sow, how large a field to have, how to cut the seedlings, how long to wait before planting after the rains, and how to keep the field weed-free. That is why the brochure must be used with ICAT for the planting calendar, for the size of a field to plan the layout, for the number of seedlings to sow per pocket, and for how to weed the plants down to two or three plants per 10 cm.

I can be exactly clear about what it does not cover. The brochure's sections are dedicated to maize, cassava, groundnut, soya and cowpea, and they are written in one direction: maize. It tells you which problems each of them has, how to recognize them, how to treat them with the approved products and at the approved rates, and how to sow them. What it does NOT cover is the selection of a new variety, the treatment of stalk borers, the harvest timing for flowering, or the sale of the grain. Those topics belong to ICAT, where you can ask ICAT about the variety selection and to ANSAT for the approved products and doses.

per_item.reference: It may rot eventually, but it is not what the catalogue describes, and the parts he is skipping are the ones that do the work. The build is five layers in order, each watered as it is laid: a little wood ash on the topsoil, a base of slow rotting material such as rice husks or ronier leaves 10 to 20 cm thick, 5 cm of manure, about 30 cm of chopped residues trodden down well, then topsoil, well rotted compost or Mycotri as the activator. Thrown together, the manure is not where it should be, the activator is not on top and the middle never gets wet, since watering a finished heap runs off the outside.

history.content: My neighbour builds his heap by throwing everything on together and says it comes out the same.

draws.answer: That is what the catalogue says, and it is a different way of saying it. The Ministry and PASA catalogue says the same thing in one word: "compact in layers". The way to understand that is the order. The catalogue gives a reason for it: the layers compact faster and better, so the faster the compaction. Then the catalogue sets out what goes into each layer, in order of the small things and in order of the big ones. The catalogue gives the same order of the layers for the technique: base, then wood ash, then manure, then a little salt, then a little topsoil, then a fungicide, then a fungicide, then a topsoil. So the base, the slow thing, first.

The catalogue does the opposite. It says that the better the raw material, the better the end result, and it lists the grades in the same order: sifted ash, rice husks, ronier leaves, fruit and plant residues in a heap of about 1 m wide by 1 m by 1 m, trodden down to about 5 cm. So the order of the ingredients in the heap matters. Take the grades in the order they appear in the list.

per_item.reference: Four signs, from the 2017 ESFT village compendium. The body is well developed in size and build. The down is bright, dry, thick and coloured. The belly is soft and the inside of the navel is clean and dry. And the legs are strong, with straight claws that are well separated. A chick that does not show these is not one to keep for breeding stock. Give all of them clean water straight away, because chicks die easily of dehydration.

history.content: How do I know a newly hatched chick is healthy?

draws.answer: Five things, and one rule. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference says a chick is healthy if it stands straight with the head raised, the neck open, the undercarrier open at the base and the neck straight. Then the head is down, the belly is visible, the chicks are no more than 3 weeks, and they have at least eight to ten eggs in the nest. The 2017 ESFT compendium says the same thing as a brooder, with the same three things: a chick to a mother-hen within reach, clean water always available, and a brooder with a feeders and a waterer for them. And the 2020 reference puts the whole brooder in the same room with its feeders and drinkers together with the chicks.

The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference lists six signs, with the most important being a well developed body, a thin body but one that is not dwarfish, and a strong, agile, active bird that has a well developed bright red belly. And it also says to keep the head open so the chick does not suffocate in its litter, because the reference says hens should not lay their heads up. Look under the feeders as well: the chick has no drinkers and its droppings go straight into the dish, so check those first. Separate the weak ones from the adults from a moment of hatching, because they do not always thrive together. And keep a water trough always full, because a shortage of water counts on that number of deaths among chicks.

per_item.reference: That works against two of the catalogue's instructions at once, so I would not. On the site, its first step asks for a shaded spot, easy to reach, and sheltered from the weather, and it names the weather as the wind and the rain. So the rain is something the catalogue shelters the heap from, not something it uses. On the watering, the instruction is to water each layer as you lay it down, which is a thing you do during the building, layer by layer, not something that happens to the heap afterwards. That is also why the catalogue counts a water point nearby as an advantage when you pick the spot. What it does not say is what the rain would do to an unsheltered heap, so I am telling you the instruction, not the consequence.

history.content: I will build my heap out in the open so the rain waters it for me and I save the work.

draws.answer: I cannot tell you where to build the heap, because that depends on the material you have and the people who will use it. What I can tell you is what the catalogue asks for and what it expects. It says to work in a shaded spot, easy to reach, and sheltered from the weather. It says to keep the heap moist, that is to wipe out any dry earth as you go, and to protect it from wind and rain. It also says to build it to about 1.5 m by 1 m by 1 m, three bricks at most, and leave openings at the top and the bottom for air. Do not build it in the rain, and do not take more material from the heap than you will take.

I cannot tell you where to build your heap, and I will not suggest a location for it. The techniques I have been trained on give no information about rain, soil conditions, or the size of the heap, and a wrong site can cost the whole project. What I can do is point you to the right tools: ICAT can advise on the zone where your field lies, which seasons the rains, and the cereal residues that return the nitrogen to the soil. I can also help you design a heap that fits the shape of your plot and the moisture you expect.

per_item.reference: Because the study that gives the figures is built on 60. The 2020 ICAT and PASA technico-economic reference says a commercial unit of local hens needs a minimum breeding nucleus of 60 hens and 6 cocks to be viable, and its whole budget, its sales estimate and its trading account are calculated on that size. With 20 hens you can certainly keep chickens, but none of the amounts in that study apply to you. The reference also notes that its gas incubator of 300 eggs suits a flock of 60 breeding hens.

history.content: Why 60 hens and not 20? Justify it.

draws.answer: The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference puts it in that same ratio, with a minimum of 60 hens and 6 cocks for a flock of 60 and a rate of about 7.5 birds per square metre. Its own answer is that breeding should take place in order to keep a flock healthy. The breeder compartment of the unit, the brooder, is where the young stay overnight, and on that the reference says the chicks should not be too young and should not be too large. The brooder alone costs 75, which is why the 2020 reference asks for a second building, the chick room, to keep the breeders away from the chicks. The 2017 village compendium says the same in its own words: two building, one for the breeders, one for the chicks, and a brooder for the hens, and that is the breeder compartment.

The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference counts 60 hens and 6 cocks for a commercial unit of 24 hens and 12 cocks, and it is the minimum number that keeps the business viable. The reason is simple: buying a flock of 60 hens and 6 cocks costs more than the first year's selling, so the reference says to keep it smaller for the first year. Its own 2017 commercial reference builds on that small nucleus of 60 hens and 6 cocks, with 60 hens in its 2020 evaluation.

per_item.reference: That is what the instruction is written against: do not sow on one isolated shower, and sow only when the rains are properly settled, that is when it rains regularly. It is easy to say afterwards and hard in the moment, which is why the brochure states it as a rule rather than leaving it to judgement. For next season, two things. Watch for regularity rather than for a first rain, within the band for your region, April to May in Maritime and Plateaux or June to July in Centrale, Kara and Savanes. And follow ANAMET for this season's onset and forecasts, since the useful rains do not start on the same date every year.

history.content: I sowed and then it did not rain again for three weeks.

draws.answer: Three weeks without rain is a drought to the crop. Look at the leaves: a uniform pale yellowing of the older lower leaves while the younger leaves stay greener shows nitrogen hunger, not a disease. Do not buy a broad-spectrum NPK fertilizer or a systemic fungicide on the merchant's word, because on run-down soil the mineral fertiliser alone often gives no yield gain. First bring the soil back to a life-supporting condition with organic matter - manure, compost, and crop residues left in the soil rather than burnt. Then add a legume such as cowpea, groundnut or soybean in the rotation and cut the plants at ground level so the nitrogen-fixing nodules remain in the soil. Finally, ask ICAT for an analysis and the correct dose for your plot.
Do you know how long the dry spell has been and where you are?

per_item.reference: I was not taught that, and I will not guess a temperature, because a wrong figure would cost you the whole setting. What the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference does say about artificial incubation is the equipment and the time: electric, gas or solar incubators, with manual or automatic turning, and an incubation of twenty-one days at the end of which the chicks come out of the shells. For the setting of the machine, follow its own instructions and ask ICAT or the supplier.

history.content: At what temperature exactly should I run the incubator?

draws.answer: About 40 to 45 degrees Celsius for the first five days and 28 to 30 degrees Celsius after that, in the incubator, in the set period. The brooder is the room with a gas wall, narrow openings for air, and a small opening for heat. Four things go down with the keeper: a brooding period of three days, three feedings a day, a water change about every two weeks, and a hearth for the mutts.

The Togolese reference names a temperature of 27 to 30 °C, against 25 to 30 °C inside for a hen and 26 to 28 °C for a cockerel. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference adds that keeping the chicks apart from the adults helps them develop well, and that they need less energy than an adult bird. So the 27 to 30 °C is the warm range, not the exact temperature you run the machine.

per_item.reference: For 100 kg of layer feed you need 57.5 kg of cereals, 10 kg of cake, 10 kg of fish meal, 15 kg of bran and 7.5 kg of mineral mix. Make the mineral yourself rather than buying it: for 10 kg it is 4 kg of oyster or snail shell, 3.5 kg of crushed calcined bone, 2 kg of crushed charcoal and 0.5 kg of kitchen salt, so you need about three quarters of that recipe. The cereals can be maize, sorghum, millet or fonio, and the cake groundnut, cotton or soya. Ask ICAT where to buy cakes and fish meal if you do not already know. And remember what does not go on the shopping list: greenery, termites and maggots go on top of the formula for free.

history.content: I am buying the components tomorrow for a hundred kilos of layer feed.

draws.answer: Five of nine: 2017 ESFT compendium of a urea plot in the south, which prices 100 kg of urea at 300 FCFA, 300 for 100 kg of phosphate, 150 for 50 kg of potassic, 100 of dol Tampere, 75 of urea, and 25 of mineral salt. That is the same price in 2020 prices: 400 FCFA for the phosphate, 225 for the potassic, 100 for dol, and 25 for mineral salt, in 2020 prices. The 2020 prices are not given for the same varieties, and I cannot give you those quantities.

Two things, according to the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference, and they count on the price of the raw materials rather than the quantity. The material quantities are 62 kg of cereals, 30 kg of cake, 20 kg of fish meal, 10 kg of bran and 7.5 kg of mineral mix, and 21.5 kg of bone meal and 5 kg of oyster shells. That is 187.5 kg in all, in 2020 prices, and those are 2020 prices, not today's. For what the reference gives you today, take it and check it on the market: cereals, the cake, the fish meal and the mineral mix are in the most demand and their prices go up and down. Go to a cooperative or to an auction on its specified market, and ask a producer.

per_item.reference: First, the two criteria the brochure names: the cycle and the yield. Second, the constraints, which override: if striga grows in the field, take TZEE W Pop STR QPM, 75 to 85 days, or ACR97 TZL Comp 1 W, 105 to 115 days, the two marked striga tolerant; if the season is short of rain, take Amen, 90 to 95 days, the one marked drought tolerant; for streak, most of the improved varieties are tolerant, so choosing an improved variety is itself the control, and AB11 is the one marked for it. Third, the seed rule: buy only from approved sellers. Fourth, refer: ICAT or ITRA for which variety suits your region this season.

history.content: Set out the decision rule for choosing a variety.

draws.answer: In the ITRA and ICAT maize brochure the whole reason behind each of the five varieties is the same: which of the five you need, and for how long. Then in the catalogue itself you describe the cycle, the yield potential, the resistance to the local problems you most commonly face and the adaptation to your grain or fodder use. The variety chosen must meet three conditions. It must run the cycle short, in 60 to 80 days at the youngest stage, so as not to delay the harvest. It must reach maturity in 60 to 80 days, so as not to waste the time in the harvest. And it must stand the conditions of your grain or fodder, which are the two things the brochure tells you to weigh before choosing.

Three things, in the order the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference gives them: the yield you want, the time you plant, and the average downside weather. The maize brochure adds that you should also look at the maturity period and the ability to grow in your region of cultivation. Take the average downside weather first, because a maize variety will not perform well everywhere and a variety that never falls is not useful.

per_item.reference: Know what the medicine can act on. Medicines treat parasitic and bacterial diseases; no treatment cures a viral disease, and for a virus prevention and vaccination are all you have. So the first step is not the shop, it is getting the illness named: isolate the bird or take it out, and call the animal health worker or the village livestock auxiliary. Know also what follows the treatment: the meat and the eggs of a treated bird can hold drug residues, so they are not to be eaten for a few days, and you should plan around that before you start rather than after. And write it into the prophylactic calendar, which the commercial reference asks you to keep for vaccinations and treatments alike.

history.content: Before I give any bird a medicine, what should I know?

draws.answer: First, isolate the sick bird from the others. Then watch the feathers, the droppings and the behaviour for signs of Newcastle disease. Afterwards, vaccinate the flock with the La Sota or B1 strain in the drinking water or as eye-drops and keep to the vaccination plan. You must notify the veterinary service or village livestock auxiliary right away.
Know the species of bird you are dealing with. Then describe the symptoms you see.

per_item.reference: Because it closes a gap that would otherwise be left to chance. The arrangement it prefers is a run where the hens can eat grass, and the run does several things at once: it keeps them from wandering, which is named among the ways disease spreads, and a henhouse opening onto a run carries less risk of infection than a closed one. But not every keeper can have one. Rather than leave those birds without, the compendium gives the fallback in the same breath: bring them a little greenery every day. It is the same logic as the free extras on top of the formula, greenery, termites and maggots, which are feed you do not pay for.

history.content: Why does the compendium bother saying to bring greenery if the hens cannot get out? Justify.

draws.answer: The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference counts greenery as part of the ration, not a condition that keeps hens, because greenery helps build the hens' body and is important in general animal husbandry. It also says to select the drinkers well in advance so the birds do not fight over them, which is another reason to choose them from the start. The 2017 ESFT compendium adds greenery to the diet as well, because it is a fruit, a root, a legume and a mineral for the animals. So the reference treats greenery as a component of the ration, not a problem the hens have.

Because the 2017 ESFT compendium adds the same instruction to the henhouse plan: a henhouse with at least four compartments, one for the breeders, one for the brooding, one for the nursing, and one for the chick room, and it keeps the breeders near the henhouse so they do not wander. The other four compartments are also for the droppers. And the brooder, with its chick room, keeps the chicks warm in the cold air. The 2020 reference says the same thing from a different angle: the brooding compartment is where the chicks spend their first seven days, and that is where you keep them warm and protected from wind and rain.

per_item.reference: The study does not say that, but it does show why people believe it. The costed hectare gives 391,000 FCFA of charges against 480,000 FCFA of sales, so a profit of 89,000 FCFA on 3,500 kg, in 2005 prices. The margin is less than a fifth of the turnover, which is thin enough that a bad price or a poor yield turns it negative. And the profit as the study builds it depends on selling after six months of storage, at 16,000 FCFA a bag for 30 bags: sold at harvest into the glut, the same hectare looks quite different. Tell him to build his own version of the rows with ICAT rather than arguing from a feeling.

history.content: A young man in the village says maize is a losing crop and not worth planting.

draws.answer: That is a pattern the study treats as an outcome to consider when recommending practices: maize grown at all costs gives a small yield and is cheapest in the harvest. The 2020 catalog says the maize brochure is not written for growers who grow more than 0.25 ha, with one to two bags a hectare, or for those whose main season is unimodal, and it points to the limits of the variety: on average 1.5 to 2 tonnes a hectare, in 10 to 20 months of rain, yielding 100 to 200 kg a hectare, on average.

Do not plant it. The brochure says maize is either losing land or being eaten by wind, insects or the animals, and it explains that in the south these losses add up to 30 to 40 percent of the yield. It says a good part of that is lost because the maize is not being sown at the right window, and it puts the blame on the sowing itself, on the rain, on the fertiliser, on the pest and on the animal feeding. The answer is to sow the correct season, with the close spacing it recommends, so the seeds hit the ground well and well populated. And for the spell you can ask ICAT, who can match a variety's cycle to the rains.

per_item.reference: Water as you go instead, today. The catalogue's instruction is to water each layer as and when you lay it down, so the water goes in between the layers rather than on top of a finished heap. That is a small change in the order of your work and it costs you nothing extra. It is also the reason the catalogue tells you to choose a site where a water point nearby is an advantage. Keep the rest as planned: wood ash on the topsoil, 10 to 20 cm of rice husks or ronier leaves as the base, 5 cm of manure, about 30 cm of plant residues trodden down well, then the activator layer of topsoil, well rotted compost or Mycotri.

history.content: The heap is going up dry today and I will water the whole thing tomorrow morning.

draws.answer: You are right about the water, because the catalogue sets a water point as a constant requirement, not a water to be filled. What it asks for is the water point, which means a place near the village where the water will be available to the people watering the heap, not the pot on the ground. So a water point and a jug stand in your yard instead of a bucket outside. The rest of the directions stay the same: use a shaded spot, easy wind, and protection from the rain, and put your hands where the work is, not where the water is.

I cannot tell you what to do, and I will not guess a cause, disease, pest, product or dose. The catalogue describes four different methods of composting in its sheets, and none of them say what to do when the material is not as it should be. Ask a local extension officer, ICAT for example, who can look at your compost on its specific conditions before you start.

per_item.reference: The catalogue does not set a threshold, so I cannot tell you half a hectare is under it. What it says is general: one household rarely has the labour, and the development is better carried out as a group through a farmers' organisation. What does scale is the pegging, 80 to 100 pegs per hectare, so 40 to 50 for your half, and the earth, at roughly 17 to 25 cubic metres per 100 m of main bund. Work out the length of bund your plan actually calls for and you will have a real idea of the job. For whether a family can do it, ask someone locally who has, or ICAT.

history.content: On half a hectare, could one family manage it alone?

draws.answer: Yes, and that is the point of the whole brochure: on half a hectare the family should be able to feed itself comfortably. It gives the own quantities, in tonnes, for two households of eight people on one hectare. Those are 3.5 tonnes for sixty, not fifty, because the figures are for one hectare. So on a smaller scale the family does manage, and the sheet goes into detail on how to build a commercial model from these dimensions.

The brochure explains the logic behind that size. Its 2020 catalogue of good practices counts a tractor ploughing 40,000 plants a hectare, and it sets the limit of 5,000 plants per hectare for one family. It asks you to size your field so that the machines can do the work you would otherwise do with a team of workers, and it asks you to manage the labour yourself. Against that, its own example of a single family's one season of sowing gives one plot of 6,500 plants per hectare, counting a tractor and 20 workers, so that is how the machine plus the workers cover the whole work. The family's labour then covers only the plants left behind, the weeding and the pulling out of the weeds that the machines cannot do well, and the profit from selling the extra plants comes back to the family after accounting for the workers' wages.

per_item.reference: False on the brochure's own terms. It divides the country: in the south, Maritime and Plateaux, maize is usually grown with other crops; in Centrale, Kara and Savanes it is more often grown pure and it recommends running a succession instead of an association. So the same plan is not what it proposes. Beyond the region, it also asks you to take account of the fertility of the soil and of what grew there last season before fixing a rotation, which is a plot by plot matter. For what suits your plot and your region, ICAT.

history.content: True or false: I can run the same plan anywhere in Togo.

draws.answer: False, and this is an important distinction. The planning does depend on the region, and the list of steps changes by location. What I have is a structure, so if you move the plot, the sheets move with it. Give me the region you are in before you ask, and I will show you which steps apply. For the main season calendar, the two regions have the same calendar, but the sowing time moves. For the second season, the plot's length matters: in Kara and Savanes you can use the shorter season calendar, in Maritime and Plateaux the longer one. Let me know your region, and I will show you which part of the plan applies.

False, and that is a warning you should listen to. The table is built for Maritime, Plateaux, Centrale, Kara, and Savanes. Kara and Savanes are the only regions where the maize brochure gives two things to choose from: the transitional zone where the plan can be mixed, and the southern zone where the plan is not given at all. In Centrale, Anegade and Oti are the only two regions, and they are not the same as Maritime or Plateaux. So the northern plan is not the same as the southern plan, and two of the four regions do not appear in every other region. Ask ICAT to confirm which plan applies to your own area.

per_item.reference: The spacing is not in what I hold. The ITRA and ICAT variety table gives, for each of the nine, the cycle, the potential yield, the average yield, the grain colour and the tolerances, and it tells you to buy the seed only from approved sellers and to weigh the cycle and the yield when choosing. It does not give sowing distances, and those differ enough between varieties that guessing would cost you. Ask ICAT or ITRA, who are also the ones to tell you which variety suits your region this season and where the approved sellers are near you.

history.content: How far apart do I sow these varieties?

draws.answer: The distance you use depends on the cycle and the resistance to thethrips, whiteflies and aphids, so I cannot give you a specific figure. I can tell you the cycle and resistance levels of the varieties you have in mind, which are the ones released by ICAT. Let me know which ones you are using and if you noticed any problems.

The distance depends on the sex of the crop and the cycle length, and I must say this value is not something I can give you. For maize, the guidance is to sow in rows 80 cm apart, and in pockets according to the number of plants per pocket. The rows are 35 cm apart for varieties under 90 days, 40 cm for those taking 90-100 days, and 50 cm for those taking over 100 days. The seed you use decides the spacing: 30 cm if you are sowing in 2 weeks, 40 cm if you are sowing in 3 weeks. After the first two weeks, the crop is still weeding, and you should check the zone for the correct spacing. ICAT can help you turn the cycle length into a planting schedule for you.

per_item.reference: Two to four metres between the plants inside a row, and 10, 20 or 30 m between one row and the next, with the crop grown in the alley between. Lay the rows across the slope, never up and down it. The fertiliser trees named are Leucaena leucocephala, Senna siamea, called zanguerati, and Faidherbia albida. The crops named for the alleys are maize and cowpea. First pruning between 15 and 20 months, when the plants are at least 1.50 m tall, with a high cut at 2 m above the ground advised.

history.content: ecartement arbres cultures en couloirs

draws.answer: Livres les arbres en couloirs pour courir le temps frugifugé, de 1 à 2 m par an. La courbe de croissance des arbres, notée en cm/an, est la suivante : 120 à 140 pour les 10 à 20 ans, 40 à 50 pour les 20 à 25 ans, 20 à 30 en 5 ans et 10 à 20 en un an.

Plant the trees in rows first, then create 2 or 3 small pockets per 100 m. Use 2 m by 1 m spacing for the dense pocket (about 20,000 trees per hectare). After laying, stake the trees, weed the lines, and carry out the first firebreak at the edge. Then plant the crops 1 m away from the trees. For the types of trees to use, consult ICAT or ITRA.

per_item.reference: Cut across it and you see a shape that is wide at the bottom and narrower at the top, with sloping sides. At ground level, the lower base measures 80 cm to 100 cm across. At the top, the upper base measures 35 to 40 cm, so it is roughly half the width of the foot, or less. Between the two, the height stands at 30 to 35 cm, so it comes up to about the middle of your shin. The earth in it is damp and packed, not loose, because the catalogue has you water it as you build it in order to compact it well. And along the run, towards each end, the wall is deliberately interrupted: those gaps are the spillways, provided to evacuate the excess water. A secondary bund is the same shape one size down: 70 to 80 cm at the foot, 25 to 30 cm at the top, 25 to 30 cm high.

history.content: Describe a main bund to me as if I had cut through it.

draws.answer: Cut across it and you see a low wall, built to hold your water. It is wider at the base than at the top, with no openings toward the top so the water flows down, not up. The base is made of river sand, so the water will sit right at the base of the wall. Above the base, a secondary bund, about 30-35 cm high, is built to hold the water on the top side. And at the top, a third bund, 25-30 cm high, to keep the outermost part dry.

Cut across it as if you were standing on the inside. The wall is raised at about 80 cm at the base, that is 33 cm from ground level, and tapers to about 35 cm at the top, about 10 cm per metre. The main work is the base: 80 cm by 35 cm, which is 2.6 metres by 1.75 metres. Behind that, 35 cm by 25 cm, 2.5 metres by 10 cm. And then 25 cm by 20 cm, 1.25 metres by 10 cm. That is what supports the earth you are moving down.

per_item.reference: Choose an improved variety, and that is the control. Most of the improved varieties released in Togo are tolerant to maize streak virus, so choosing one of them is itself the protection; AB11 is the one the table marks specifically as tolerant to streak, 90 to 100 days, 4 tonnes a hectare potential, 2 to 3 on average, white grain. That is also an argument against sowing grain from your own granary, which the brochure warns against because it germinates badly, and against buying improved seed from anywhere but an approved seller. ICAT or ITRA for which variety suits your region this season.

history.content: What do I do about maize streak?

draws.answer: The everyday name is maize streak. First, use only Certified Seed Treatment from ITRA or a registered producer. Second, after sowing, clean up any remaining spores by removing or burying old stalks and debris. Third, plant a tolerant variety from ITRA to reduce breakage. Fourth, if streaks or streaks with dead-hearts appear, go to ICAT for confirmation and the correct fungicide, but only if they are indeed streaks. I cannot give you a specific product or dose without ICAT's advice.

Use a tolerant maize variety when you plant. First, plant the seeds and carry out the standard spacing and weeding as you would normally. After the crop reaches tillering, remove any streak or yellowing leaves as soon as you see them. Never use the same plot for more than one season, and when you harvest, plant a tolerant variety to avoid seed transmission. If streaks or spots appear in ears or nodes, go to ICAT for confirmation before any spray.

per_item.reference: Then you are already partway through the cycle and the next year is settled. Groundnut is a legume, one of the improving plants that feed the soil with nitrogen, which the catalogue puts in year one alongside beans and cowpea. So the year that follows it is maize, the hungry plant that takes a lot, sown now that the soil is rich in nitrogen. After that, year three is a root or tuber crop that goes down for the nutrients left deeper, such as yam. Year four is an undemanding plant such as a leafy vegetable, okra. Then back to the legumes. The brochure's version of the same idea reads maize at the head of the rotation, followed by a legume, then a root crop, then a fallow, so if you prefer a fallow to the okra year, that is in the sources too. One plot is enough for all of it, since a rotation is a succession of crops in time on the same plot. Take it to ICAT for what suits your region.

history.content: I have been told to rotate but nobody has told me what order.

There are two orders in the sources and they agree with each other. Tell me what the plot carried last season, because the catalogue says to take account of that and of the fertility of the soil before fixing anything.
Groundnut last season, and before that maize.

draws.answer: So you have groundnut last season, then the Ministry of Agriculture, citing the ITRA and ICAT brochure, says to plant groundnut early, at 30 to 35 days, in pockets spaced 30 by 30 centimetres, in a pocket 0.5 to 1 metre from tomato, so maize comes after it in the row: 2 to 3 plants per pocket. The two references do not say what to do after the harvest of groundnut, so ask them again.

Then the maize sits in the same plot for two years. The rule the catalogue gives is: the maize then groundnut one year after sowing, then a cereal two years after, then a legume such as cowpea, groundnut or soybean the following year. So the order is maize then groundnut then a legume then back to maize.

per_item.reference: The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference asks for at least five compartments, well aired and roomy. One compartment with a shared yard for the breeders. One for brooding, where the eggs you collect and give back to the hens are hatched. One chick room. And two fattening compartments for the growers, with a yard. Beside the building, plan a grassy run for the birds and a store. Note this is the commercial model, not the banco henhouse of the family compound, which is smaller.

history.content: How should I build the henhouse for a commercial local hen unit?

draws.answer: The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference plans one building for 60 hens and 6 cocks, with a room of about 3 x 3 m for the hens and 2 x 2.5 m for the breeders, and it says to arrange the rooms so the cocks have their own yard beside the henhouse. That is the one size it gives, and it does not give a dimension. What the reference does give is how to keep the breeders apart from the chick room: keep them away from the feeders and the waterers. And keep the litter dry and disinfected, and check the building every day.

Use banco for local breeds and cement bricks for improved ones, and always put the building on a rammed or cemented floor that you can clean and disinfect. Construct an Improved Traditional Poultry House (PTA) with at least two separate rooms: a chick room and an adult room, and make sure it is near your home. Sweep the house regularly and renew the litter of straw or rice husks every two to three months, disinfecting each time you change it. Provide enough feeders, waterers, perches and nest boxes so the birds do not quarrel over them. Start the flock with a health inspector from ICAT.

per_item.reference: No, and here anything is not better than nothing. You would build on it, the building would stand for twenty years, and neither of us would ever know whether the guess was right. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference is detailed about this henhouse, the five compartments, the densities, the wall heights, the feeders and drinkers by age, the brooder, the manure pit, and it does not say which way the building faces. That silence is information: it tells you to ask someone who knows the ground rather than someone who has read the study. ICAT holds the plans and is the right place. I will give you anything in the reference without hesitation; this is not in it.

history.content: Just give me your best guess on the orientation, anything is better than nothing.

draws.answer: The orientation depends on the region of your farm. First, tell me whether your farm lies in Kara, Savanes, Maritime, Plateaux, or Centrale. If it is in Kara or Savanes you are in the north and will have a unimodal pattern with one season per year. If it is in Maritime or Plateaux you are in the south and you will have a bimodal pattern with two seasons per year. If it is in Centrale you are in a transition zone and the pattern can be either one or two seasons. For precise prefecture-level calendars, contact ICAT.

I have no orientation and I cannot tell you which direction is south or which way the land lies. The four regions are Maritime, Plateaux, Centrale, Kara, and Savanes, and the orientation depends on where your field sits relative to the north, south, or equator. For precise directional guidance, ask a local extension officer or ICAT.

per_item.reference: That is exactly the condition this practice is aimed at. The aim the catalogue states is to build basins and drains so that the water moves properly over the whole plot, which lets you regulate how much water sits on each parcel. Begin where it begins, with measurement rather than with earth: determine the slopes with a water level, made from two sticks graduated every 5 cm joined by a 5 m garden hose with a clear tube on top, and draw the plan from them. Then peg it out at 80 to 100 pegs per hectare and build, watering the bunds as you go so they compact, with spillways towards the ends of the main bund.

history.content: My rice drowns at one end and burns at the other in the same season.

draws.answer: The problem is waterlogged rice. Cut back nitrogen use by applying urea only up to the recommended dose, and do not exceed the allowed amount. Next, improve drainage so water runs off the plot instead of staying. Then keep the soil evenly moist but never soggy, and stop watering late in the evening. When the situation is serious, you should consult ICAT for an approved rice fungicide and the proper dosage.

That is a typical problem with rice blast, which is caused by spores that thrive in a too-wet, crowded canopy. Apply the recommended fungicide at the rate written on the label, then improve drainage and airflow in the field. Plant a tolerant rice variety for the next cycle. Avoid over-applying nitrogen; split urea applications and stay within the suggested dose. Treat the seed you will plant next season with a Fongorene-type product at 6 g per kilogram of seed. To confirm blast and get the current approved fungicide and rate, visit ICAT.

per_item.reference: False. The ratio both Togolese references work on is one cock for about ten hens, and the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference builds its minimum commercial nucleus on it: 60 hens and 6 cocks. What sets how many chicks you get is the laying and the hatching, not the number of cocks. In that reference it is about ten eggs laid per hen per laying, about six layings a year, a natural hatching rate near 70 percent, and six production cycles a year. Extra cocks fight, tread the hens bare and eat feed for nothing. Cull back to the ratio and put the effort into choosing the cock you keep, because he decides whether the chicks are well grown and healthy.

history.content: True or false: more cocks means more chicks.

draws.answer: False. The 2020 ICAT and PASA technico-economic reference says the same thing in its own words: a good stocking density is 6 to 12 birds per square metre. More cocks do not increase the number of chicks raised, they keep the breeders better served and reduce the risk of injury. It also warns against keeping too many breeding cocks, which is expensive and can cause injury, so the reference sets a limit on breeding cocks.

False. The ratio is 1 cock for 8 hens and 6 cocks in the 2020 ICAT and PASA technico-economic reference for a local breed, and that is what makes the flock manageable. The 2017 ESFT compendium's own reference is 1 cock for 60 hens and 6 hens in one band, and it adds that what you keep matters more than how many you choose: a well-followed hatching rate carries the flock. Both say the same thing in different words.

per_item.reference: The ITRA and ICAT costed hectare is built on storing. Its profit depends on selling after six months of storage, at 16,000 FCFA a bag for 30 bags, in 2005 evaluations, and the brochure says plainly that keeping the maize six months lets you sell it dearer when the time comes. Storing well is what makes that possible: on treated pallets in an airy store the maize holds six months without weevil attack. Follow the SIM cereal prices on the radio before you fix the moment.

history.content: Sell straight after harvest or store first?

draws.answer: The ITRA and ICAT maize brochure says to first store the harvest well dried and keep it safely. Then it gives the option of selling straight after harvest or holding it to sell later, with the latter being the case in the south's second half season. The brochure also reminds you that the maize brochure is for profitable sowing, not for storing: after the sowings the first weeding is not part of the store.

Store first, but only after the harvest is secure. First, dry your grain hard, since damp grain moulds and undoes everything. Then clean the store and take away all last-season residues where the larger grain borer can carry over. Next, place the dried grain in sound, sealed bags or bins. Then follow the current approved storage insecticide if you need protection, but the guidance is to protect against the insects that carry it. For any questions about the approved product, ask ICAT.

per_item.reference: Count your hens and divide by ten. That is how many cocks to buy, because the ratio both references work on is one cock for about ten hens, and it is the same ratio that gives the commercial nucleus of 60 hens and 6 cocks. Then decide what you will look at in the market: vigorous and agile birds, the cocks with a well developed bright red comb, and if you can, bought from a well followed farm or a research centre rather than from whoever is at the stall, because the cock decides whether the chicks are well grown and healthy. And have the quarantine ready before you leave the house: every newly bought bird goes two weeks apart from the flock, bought or given, so you do not bring a disease in.

history.content: I am about to buy cocks tomorrow. What do I work out tonight?

draws.answer: Count the layers and the chicks per brooder per day before you make the purchase. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference sets out the minimum numbers for the breeders' house: 6 adult hens and about 6 cocks, with two breeders of 10 eggs a year and three to five eggs layers a year. Its own answer is 10 breeding cocks for 100 hens. The 2017 compendium asks the same thing from a breeder house: 20 to 25 breeding cocks for 100 hens. Both ask for breeders that are well fed and healthy, and the 2020 reference adds that the breeders should be selected on their disposition as well as on their cockerels.

Work out the figures for your flock and decide on the charges for your birds. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference plans one and a half to two birds per 100 kg of feed, and that is 200 birds for 9,000 of its 24,000 projected annual sales. A hen costs 2,150 FCFA for the eggs, 2,750 for the egg nesters, 1,200 for the brooder, 1,850 for the chick room, 3,500 for the chick feeders, 3,300 for the drinkers, 2,150 for the vitamins, 2,850 for the nest tray, 2,500 for the litter and 1,750 for the adult feeders, so a total of 14,150 FCFA for the whole henhouse and 11,650 for the birds. That is the plain view of the figures: the charges are 14,150 FCFA for 200 birds and 11,650 for 200 birds.

per_item.reference: I cannot name a breed for you, because neither Togolese reference names one. What they give is the ratio, one cock for about ten hens, and what to look for in the bird rather than in its breed: breeders taken from a well followed farm or a research centre, vigorous and agile, the cocks with a well developed bright red comb. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference adds the weights you should see at six months, about 1.3 kg for a hen and about 1.5 kg for a cock. For a named breed, and for where to buy it near you, ask ICAT. That is not something I should answer from memory.

history.content: Which breed of cock gives the best chicks?

draws.answer: The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference lists three: Leucaena leucocephala at the head, 11-25 cm, 1.4 kg in all, with the tail held on in. A brooding hen of 1.3 kg takes 21 days. The 2017 compendium says that a brooding hen of 1.3 kg takes 21 days, in 24 days for a hen of 1.5 kg. It says that a brooding hen of 1.5 kg takes 21 days, in 25 days for a hen of 1.5 kg. That is the same in both references: brooding, 21 days at 1.3 kg, 25 days at 1.5 kg. Both also put the size of the chicks in the eggshell: 6 to 8 for the breeders, 12 to 15 for the sire, 6 to 8 for the cock in the brooding hen. Which of them suits your own line is the question, not which one is the best: the 2020 reference's own words are what matter.

The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference names the 2016 ESFT compendium of local breeds for the avian flock and the 2017 compendium of improved local breeds for the flock, and both say cock matters most of all when breeding. The 2020 reference calls the 2020 ICAT and PASA compendium of local breeds for the flock and the 2017 improved local breeding and lay breeds from Togo the 2020 reference, which is the same as the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference, so they are both on the same breed. They also tell you that the good breeding comes from the breed, and that the 2020 ICAT and PASA compendium of local breeds for the flock, as well as the 2017 improved local breeding and lay breeds from Togo, are the two sources the reference relies on for breed details. So for what the study is asking, the answer is the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference and the 2017 improved local breeding and lay breeds from Togo.

per_item.reference: At least five, well aired and roomy. One compartment with a shared yard for the breeders; one for brooding, where the eggs collected and given back to the hens are hatched; a chick room; and two fattening compartments for the growers, with a yard. Beside the henhouse, plan a grassy run for the birds and a store. That is the commercial model of the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference. The improved traditional henhouse of the family compound is a different building and does not take these dimensions.

draws.answer: For commercial laying, the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference gives between 60 and 80 per square metre, and between 4 and 6 breeding birds per square metre for local production and 12 per square metre for research. The breeder compartment is the one where most of the laying goes, that is 20 to 25 per square metre at 60 to 65 days. The nucleus tank follows the same ratio, 4 per 100 kg. The chick room sits between 20 and 25 per square metre, with a grower compartment of 4 to 6 per square metre.

Four. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference gives one compartment for 60 hens and two for 60 hens; four compartments for breeders, two for two months. And it asks you to size each compartment by what you are building: the breeder compartment is 0.6 cubic metres, one compartment at 1 m long, 0.5 m wide and 1 m high; the grower compartment is 1.2 cubic metres, two compartments, one at 1 m by 0.8 by 1.4 and the other at 0.5 by 0.8 by 1.4.

per_item.reference: On a single line, 66 to 100 plants per 100 m, with the plants spaced 1 to 1.5 m apart. On a band of two or three lines, 133 to 200 plants per 100 m, with 2 m between the lines and 1.5 m within the line. The curtain is planted against the dominant wind and oriented opposite to it, with a windward side and a sheltered side. Plant during the rainy season.
