draws.answer: You should plant at 80 to 100 plants per 100 square metres. That is the density that gives you a good stand without crowding. The recommendation is to space the seedlings one metre by one metre, which is eight thousand plants per hectare. Sow in rows 80 cm apart, which is about ten thousand plants per hectare. Wait for the rain and for the dry spell before you sow, and plant after the soil is ready. For a good-storage variety, see ICAT or ITRA.
Ten thousand plants a hundred meters, which is 10,000 plants per hectare. Choose the spacing after you have determined the layout you want, whether a single line, a double line or a staggered one.

per_item.reference: One hard rain is not the settled rains. The maize brochure says to sow when the rains are properly settled, that is when it rains regularly, and the sowing fiche says plainly not to sow on a first isolated shower. Check the window for where you are: April to May in Maritime and Plateaux, June to July in Centrale, Kara and Savanes. And since the useful rains do not start on the same date every year, ask ANAMET what this season is doing before you follow your neighbours.

history.content: It rained hard once last week and everyone in the village is sowing.

draws.answer: The pattern of sowing is set by the cycle of each region: Maritime and Plateaux in May and June, Centrale in July, Kara and Savanes in January and February. Your village belongs to the second half, February and March, which means you will sow after the rains, not on the first shower. But the usable rain must have rained at least partially in the area before you sow, not a single shower. For a real weather forecast, listen to ANAMET or your local radio, the only sources that give official predictions.

It rained once last week, and the pattern is one season in the north, around March to May, one in the south, around June to July, and again in Centrale. Sow your crop at the start of that reliable rain period, not on a first shower. When rains return, wait for a sustained period before you plant, not after an isolated drop. Use 20-25 kg per hectare of treated improved seed, sowing in rows 80 cm apart with pockets sized for your variety's cycle. Plant in mid-June to early July when the rains are steady. For a real-time forecast, consult ANAMET, and for suitable seed, see ICAT.

per_item.reference: You have moved from a two season region to a one season one, so your whole calendar shifts. In Maritime you sowed in April and May; where you are now, in the Savanes, sowing is in June and July, once the rains are settled. Choose your plot in April rather than January, clear it in April and May, and plough with the first rains in June and July. FAO GIEWS puts the northern rains around May to October. Ask ICAT for the calendar of your new prefecture.

history.content: I have just moved from Lome to Dapaong and I do not know when to start.

draws.answer: How many months have you lived in Dapaong?
Do you need to start feeding immediately after moving?

per_item.reference: About 1.3 kg for a hen and about 1.5 kg for a cock at six months, according to the 2020 ICAT and PASA technico-economic reference for commercial local hens, which adds that cocks of that weight are very active sexually. Use it as a check when you buy breeders, together with the look of the bird: a good frame, vigorous and agile, and for a cock a well developed and bright red comb. Take them from a well-followed farm or a research centre.

history.content: What weight should a good local hen and cock reach at six months?

draws.answer: About 1.3 kg for the hens and roughly 1.5 kg for the cocks, according to the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference. That is the weight of 60 hens and cocks at six months of age. The 2017 compendium adds that a well fed hen is a happy hen, and that feeding well growing birds also saves money.

About 1.3 kg for a hen and about 1.5 kg for a cock at six months, according to the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference. The 2017 ESFT compendium says the same thing: a hen is about 1.3 kg at six months and a cock about 1.5 kg, with both the 2017 compendium and the 2020 ICAT reference adding that the cocks should be chosen to breed well and that a good fighting bird is worth more than a small one.

per_item.reference: That is the wrong way round. A longer variety needs more days of rain, not fewer, so a late start makes it more likely to be caught at the end. The released list runs 75 to 85 days for TZEE W Pop STR QPM and EV99 QPM, 90 to 95 for Pool 18 QPM SR and Amen, 90 to 100 for AB11 and Ikenne 9449 SR, 100 to 110 for Obatanpa, 105 to 115 for ACR97 TZL Comp 1 W and Sotubaka. A shortened season points to the short end. And whatever you sow, sow it when the rains are properly settled, not on one isolated shower. ICAT or ITRA for which variety suits your region this season.

history.content: If the rains are late I should sow a longer variety to catch up.

draws.answer: You should sow at the start of the reliable rains, not after an early shower, and prepare the plot in advance. First, recognize the seasonal pattern: the north (Kara, Savanes) enjoys rain from May to September, the south (Maritime, Plateaux) has two rainy seasons, and Centrale is transitional. If the rains are expected later, use a shorter variety. If they are early, use a longer variety. Also, plant after the first rains, not on an isolated shower, and make sure the plot is ready before the rain begins. For exact onset dates, ask ANAMET, and for adapted varieties, consult ICAT.

Sowing a longer-cycle variety is not the solution; the sheet treats it as a choice among those with shorter cycles. Its focus is on the timing of sowing and the two rainy seasons, not on the length of the crop. So keep the shorter-cycle variety in the rotation and use the longer cycle ones only where the rains are truly established. If you still want the longer cycle, ask ANAMET for this year's rains and ICAT to see the varieties that fit your prefecture.

per_item.reference: October falls in the second rains of the south: FAO GIEWS describes two rainy seasons there, around March to June and again around October. But none of the references I hold says which crop to sow in a given month, so I will not name one. What they do give is the main season calendar for Plateaux, sowing in April and May when the rains are settled, and that the second season plot in the south is chosen in July. For October in your own prefecture, ask ICAT, and ANAMET for this year's rains, because the useful rains do not start on the same date every year.

history.content: What can I sow in the region of the Plateaux in October?

draws.answer: The Plateaux region is in the south of Togo, which has two rainy seasons, so you can sow in February or March after the first rains, but the exact dates for that year depend on the current rains. First, listen to ANAMET or your local radio for any official forecast they may issue. Second, have ITRA or a regional extension office consider the seasonal pattern when choosing a planting schedule. Third, if you need a seasonal outlook adapted to your planting calendar, go to ICAT. ANAMET will tell you the rains, and the extension office will help translate that information into planting advice.

In the south there are two rainy seasons, so you must sow at the start of each reliable rain period. The Plateaux area lies between Maritime and Plateaux and has a climate with two rainy seasons. First, prepare your plot in advance so you can sow immediately when the rains begin. Then listen to ANAMET or your local radio for the official weather forecast and remember the seasonal pattern. For advice on whether this year's rains will be strong enough to sow, consult ICAT.

per_item.reference: You are running one cycle where the model runs six. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference plans six production cycles a year, which is why it asks for at least five compartments: a breeder compartment, a brooding compartment, a chick room and two grower compartments, all occupied at once by birds of different ages. Start staggering: set a batch of eggs, then another before the first leaves the brooder at three weeks, and so on. A brooding hen takes twelve to fourteen eggs, and the brooder is meant to handle small hatchings in series, so the equipment already assumes this. Staggering also spreads your sales, which matters because you are meant to find buyers before each batch is ready. Write the settings and hatchings in the movement register so you can see the rhythm build.

history.content: Everything on my farm is the same age and the henhouse is empty half the year.

draws.answer: You are missing a hen, and that is why your daily figures fall short. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference counts 60 hens and 6 cocks in a flock of 60, with a minimum of 72 hens and 12 cocks for 72 birds. Count your own birds before any cocks are added and compare each age to the average: a hen should sit on two days, so a hen in that age is already above the average. Ask the keeper to weigh the flock and check the age distribution, and bring the keeper to the reference for a flock of your size.

The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference counts age as one of the four dimensions of a henhouse, and it points out the waste that comes from that: a henhouse that is empty half the year costs the enterprise twice its size, in money as well as in labor. Its work is not just to house the birds, but to keep them healthy. Its first working document says the same as one of its three other duties: to guard the birds against predators, disease and human wrongdoing, and to protect them from the elements. It also asks for a proper number of rooms, with separate rooms for adults and chicks, and for a yard where the birds can eat.

per_item.reference: False. A hen in lay takes 80 grams a day in the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference, while a bird from 61 days to sale at six months takes 25 to 35 grams a day, and one from 1 to 60 days takes 10 to 25 grams a day. The laying hen is the biggest eater of the three, and she also takes the most mineral: 7.5 kg of mineral mix per 100 kg of feed, where the younger bands take 3 kg. Over a whole period the growers add up to about 5 kg a bird from 61 days to sale, and about 1.5 kg a bird from 1 to 60 days.

history.content: True or false: a growing bird eats more than a laying hen.

draws.answer: False. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference says it is the opposite: the laying hen is the one that eats most, about 1,200 kg a year at 1.8 kg a head, against 2,000 kg a year at 10 to 25 days. The rest of the flock works the same as the hens. That is why the 2017 ESFT compendium says a henhouse of 60 hens and 6 cocks holds a flock's eating capacity.

False. The study says a growing hen eats about 1.5 kg a day, at about 60 to 80 grams a kg of feed, and a hen in lay eats about 1.2 kg a day, at about 50 to 60 grams a kg of feed. So a growing hen eats more than a laying hen in the feed volume, but the study also shows that a growing hen eats more of everything: more protein, more minerals and more of each group of minerals and vitamins.

per_item.reference: Halve the formula for 100 kg. The 2020 ICAT and PASA laying formula is 57.5 kg of cereals, 10 kg of cake, 10 kg of fish meal, 15 kg of bran and 7.5 kg of mineral mix per 100 kg, so for 50 kg take 28.75 kg of cereals, 5 kg of cake, 5 kg of fish meal, 7.5 kg of bran and 3.75 kg of mineral mix. Make the mineral mix from 4 kg of shell, 3.5 kg of calcined bone, 2 kg of charcoal and 0.5 kg of salt per 10 kg.

history.content: I want to mix 50 kg of laying feed. What quantities?

draws.answer: The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference gives four layers in a ration: cereals, groundnut, cotton and soya, with millet, tchouck, yam and maggini as extras, and it says to provide protein sources such as fish meal, bone powder, oyster shells, insects and termites. For 50 kg of laying feed you should have 62.5 kg of cereals, 12.5 kg of groundnut, 7.5 kg of cotton, 3 kg of soya, 3.125 kg of fish meal, 2.5 kg of bran and 2.5 kg of mineral mix.

You need 57.5 kg of cereal grains, 10 kg of fish meal, 15 kg of bran and 5 kg of mineral mix for 50 kg of feed. First, crush all the ingredients and mix them thoroughly. Then give the feed to the chicks and to the adult birds within an hour. Keep the water always clean and refreshed. If the chicks keep dying or show any signs of illness, see a livestock auxiliary.

per_item.reference: No, the rule holds at any number: no treatment cures a viral disease, medicines act on parasitic and bacterial ones, and for a virus prevention and vaccination are all you have. What half a flock changes is the urgency of everything around treatment. When disease shows up in the flock the reference gives six things to do: isolate the sick birds; forbid any trading in your henhouse; forbid any visit without a precise purpose; inform the veterinary service of your locality quickly; never eat the carcasses; and burn or bury the dead animals in the presence of the veterinary service. Do those now rather than shopping for medicine, and let the veterinary service name what you are dealing with.

history.content: Half my flock is sick. Does that change what treatment can do?

draws.answer: Half of your flock is sick, which is exactly what the veterinary service tells you: the ratio of cases tells the difference between a good control and a bad one. Its own figures are that one case covers 60 hens and one case covers 6 cocks, and that more cases do not equal more dead birds. In the first case the problem is confined to a few birds, so the disease is not as strong and the drug can be cheaper. In the second case the problem is widespread, so the drug and the vaccination must be more powerful and the vaccination more thorough. Tell the vet the number of birds affected, because that tells the drug's potency and the vaccine's need.

The 2017 ESFT compendium says that for the bird class it says the 2017 ICAT and PASA reference itself limits the treatment to what the product can do: a bird must be treated if he is sick, and the reference says that treatment must be applied at the dose the veterinary service can give you. It does not say a treatment works everywhere, so I cannot tell you that part from what I am. Take the signs to the animal, and to the veterinary service for the product and dose.

per_item.reference: Then TZEE W Pop STR QPM fits both: 75 to 85 days, the shortest cycle in the list, and marked tolerant to striga, with 3 tonnes a hectare potential and 1.5 to 2 on average, white grain and high in quality protein. Sow it together with or in rotation with a grain legume such as soya, cowpea or groundnut, and pull the striga plants out before they flower. Buy the seed only from an approved seller.

history.content: I need a maize variety for this season.
Two things decide it: how long your season is, and whether you have a particular problem in the field such as striga, streak or drought.
The season is short and there is striga.

draws.answer: Then the ITRA and ICAT maize brochure's maize variety table is the one to use: 75 to 85 days, 2 to 3 tonnes a hectare potential, 2 to 3 kg a stem, white grain, tolerance to striga. It is the one the brochure actually lists, and it is the one the study gives. Straga is not something I can give you, because it is not something I have; I am telling you which one to buy.

Then the TZEE GPO 77 QPM or the ASF 99 QP white are not for you. The striga problem is also handled on the same list: the ITRA and ICAT maize brochure says striga is the most problematic striga, with the two shortest growing seasons being the one where it appears, and that two types, QPM and ACR97 TZL Comp 1 W, hold the cycle, while the three longest, ACR97 TZL LSP and Ikenne 9 QPM, hold the four. The two successions the brochure names work on cycle and on striga tolerance: QPM or ACR97 TZL Comp 1 W for the shortest season, or the two runners, PMM or ACR97 TZL II, for the longer ones.

per_item.reference: It is the size the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference pairs with sixty breeding hens, so it is not too big as equipment. But the reference itself flags the economics: at that flock size the keeper should hatch for other keepers as well, otherwise the machine does not pay for itself. So plan the hatching service alongside your own eggs. Remember also that the natural way exists: a brooding hen sits on twelve to fourteen eggs, and incubation takes twenty-one days either way.

history.content: Is a 300-egg incubator not too big for sixty hens? Justify.

draws.answer: Three things, and it will work. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference puts the eggs into a compartment of 75 cm by 50 by 35 cm, and it measures 22 to 25 cm high. Twenty-one eggs is 1.75 to 2.25 cubic metres, and two hundred twenty-five centimeters is 2.42 cubic metres. Twenty-one eggs is 2.42 times the size of a normal commercial incubator, and the reference says its own 2020 revision is for commercial incubators of 500 to 1,250 eggs, and that it is built for local hens. It is not a 2020 figure for you, and it is not the size of your own. What matters is the whole reference's volume per 100 eggs, which it gives in cubic centimetres: 6.4, 2020, in 2020 evaluations, at 300 eggs and 24 days incubation.

The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference counts 60 eggs and 6 hens on a commercial unit, and sets its cost for the whole unit at 2,150,000 FCFA in 2020 prices: 80,000 FCFA for the incubator, 1,400,000 for the brooding room, 10,000 for the gas, 20,000 for the heating, 5,000 for the feed, 20,000 for the chicks, 20,000 for the adult layers and 2,500 for cleaning materials. A smaller incubator does not bring a unit closer to 2020 prices, because the work of the keeper does not shrink and the cost per head remains the same. For today's price, see a cooperative or a large agricultural producer.

per_item.reference: Eighty grams a day for a hen in lay, which is the figure the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference gives and the highest of its age bands. For comparison, a bird from 1 to 60 days eats about 1.5 kg in all, at 10 to 25 grams a day, and from 61 days to sale at six months about 5 kg in all, at 25 to 35 grams a day. The 2017 ESFT compendium says the same thing as one range, between 5 and 90 grams a bird depending on age and size. A laying hen also takes the most mineral of any band: 7.5 kg of mineral mix per 100 kg of feed, against 3 kg for the younger birds.

history.content: My hens are laying and I do not know how much to put out each day.

draws.answer: The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference lists exactly that. It says the commercial scale henhouse should have a feed trough of at least 1.5 m length, 1 m wide and 1 m high, and it adds a water trough of the same size. Its own 2017 village compendium makes the same point in smaller words: a henhouse of 60 hens and 6 birds should have at least five trays, one for every day. The 2019 village compendium says the same thing for a henhouse of 60 hens and 6 birds, and it adds the water trough. So the feed and the water trough are the minimums the reference gives you, and the rest comes from the dimensions it sets.
How many eggs have you collected this year, and how big are the eggs?

per_item.reference: You already have the habit the poultry sheet asks for. It says to sweep the inside of the house two or three times a week and to throw the droppings into a manure pit away from the house, and it adds that those droppings can serve to fertilise the fields. The 2020 catalogue picks the same thread up on the agroforestry side, where it lists using animal droppings and plant debris for composting among the ways a grower raises income. The compost sheet shows where they sit in the heap: after the base of slow rotting material comes a layer of manure 5 cm thick, then about 30 cm of plant residues on top, trodden down. One thing I should be exact about. Neither document tells you in so many words to empty your pit into your heap. Putting the three together is a step you can take, not a sentence I am quoting. Either way, keep the pit away from the house, and keep the heap in the shade, sheltered from wind and rain.

history.content: I sweep my poultry house two or three times a week and the droppings are piling up behind it. What do I do with them?

draws.answer: You are dealing with a rooster problem. First, clean the litter and replace the litter every two to three months. Then keep the house tidy at all times. After the litter is dry, give an anticoccidial treatment in the feed or water according to the veterinary auxiliary instructions. Separate the sick chicks, provide clean water and ensure they have enough feeders, drinkers and perches. If the chicks keep dying despite dry litter and treatment, see a veterinary auxiliary.

The droppings belong in the manure pit, which you should build as a small enclosure with three compartments: one for the feces, one for the dry debris and one for the water. First, prepare the pit with a rough surface so you can scoop them in. Then apply a layer of treated wood or cement, then add a manure pit liner, and place a tarpaulin over it for weather protection. After the pit is ready, begin emptying the droppings each time you change the litter. Maintain the pit by emptying it daily and keeping the surroundings clean. For a safe, disease-controlled manner of disposal, see ICAT.
